The '''historic center of Genoa''' is the core of the [[old town]] organized in the maze of alleys (''caruggi'') of medieval origin that runs – from east to west – from the hill of [[Carignano (Genoa)]] to the [[Genova Piazza Principe railway station]], close to what was once the [[Villa del Principe|Palazzo del Principe]], residence of Admiral [[Andrea Doria]]. Urbanistically, the area is part of ''Municipio I Centro-Est''.

However, the current municipal area was created by the merger, which took place on several occasions starting in the second half of the 19th century, of historic Genoa with adjacent municipalities and towns (now neighborhoods), some of which have more or less ancient historic centers of their own and have been urbanistically transformed over the years.

The major urban planning operations carried out from the first half of the 19th century to beyond the middle of the 20th century (which are difficult to replicate today, given the increased interest in the protection of historic neighborhoods by the public administration), combined with the damage that occurred during [[World War II]] (many of the old buildings were destroyed during the Allied bombing raids), partly disrupted the original fabric of the historic center. Slightly less than a quarter of the buildings (23.5 percent) date from the postwar period or later.<ref name="civis" />

== History and features ==
[[File:Via luccoli genova 02.jpg|thumb|Corner of Via Luccoli, from bottom to top the street sign (with also that of the former Prè-Molo-Maddalena delegation), the [[Escutcheon (heraldry)|heraldic shield]] of Suxilia's "''compagna''" and the [[Maddalena (Genoa)|Maddalena]] ''[[sestiere]]'' plaque]]

{{see also|History of Genoa|Sestiere}}
{{blockquote|Had the architects who built [[Genoa]] had space, had they been able to indulge their imaginations unhindered by their whims, they could not have found the infinite resources and variety of motifs, designs, and arrangements that gave the façades of their palaces their original character, introducing the unexpected grandeur into every crevice.|By [[Louis Énault]], ''Breve vision hivernale d'un voyageur normand'', 1850}}

The history of the historic core of the Ligurian capital is totally linked to the [[History of Genoa|city's history]], from the beginnings of the construction of the first dwellings of the Ligurians on the hill of Castello, to the Roman period, along the years of the [[Maritime republics|Maritime Republics]] (of which the annalist [[Caffaro di Rustico da Caschifellone]], known simply as the Caffaro, [[Annales ianuenses|kept note]]), to the patriotic and insurrectional battles of [[Young Italy]] and [[Giuseppe Mazzini]]'s [[Carbonari|Carboneria]].

The first hypotheses about the history of ancient Genoa, unrelated to mythology or propagandistic versions of its origins and pre-Roman period, date back to the 17th century (an example is Odoardo Ganducio's ''Discorso sopra l'iscrittione, ouero epitafio ritrouato a Tortona in vn marmo, d' vn decurione antico genuese'', 1614), but only with the discoveries that have occurred since the end of the 19th century and the subsequent study of the finds has a clearer (albeit partly incomplete) view of the city's real past become available. However, many of the publications describing the city's history up to the mid-19th century did not address the question of the location of the earliest settlements or the period in which they originated.<ref>Marco Milanese, ''Scavi nell'oppidum preromano di Genova: (Genova, San Silvestro 1) – Volume 1'', collana Studia archaeologica Volume 48, L'Erma di Bretschneider, 1987, ISBN 88-7062-621-0, [https://books.google.com/books?id=Ge0mrXTQVIUC&dq=genova+preromana&pg=PA19 p. 19 e sgg.]</ref> Reconstructions of past centuries did not always prove to be accurate in the light of new discoveries, and it often occurred that they contained errors, due to a lack of archaeological sources and/or an attempt to locate elements of the ancient city based on those, more modern, of Genoa visible at the time when these hypotheses were made.<ref>A cura di Piera Melli, ''La città ritrovata, Archeologia urbana a Genova 1984–1994'', Tormena Editore, 1996, pp. 33, 45 ISBN 88-86017-62-6</ref>

The habit of building on existing structures (often recycling materials salvaged from earlier constructions, even from places outside Genoa), the numerous alterations and expansions of pre-existing buildings and churches carried out during periods of economic prosperity and growth of the city, or even the outright urbanistic revolutions caused by the growing need to improve the city's road network, as well as the destruction wrought by [[Bombardment of Genoa|French bombardments]] in the 17th century, those related to the [[House of Savoy|Savoy]]'s repression of the [[Revolt of Genoa|independence uprisings of 1849]], and finally those suffered at the hands of the Allies in World War II, which were followed by related reconstructions, have given rise to a very heterogeneous building situation, with streets and squares where, within the space of a few dozen meters, buildings can be found separated from each other by centuries of history. Most of the ancient buildings that make up the historic center date back to the 12th and 13th centuries,<ref>A cura di Piera Melli, ''La città ritrovata, Archeologia urbana a Genova 1984–1994'', p. 390, Tormena Editore, 1996, ISBN 88-86017-62-6</ref> although they have often undergone later modifications.

The area of the historic center is bounded by the watersheds that divide it from the [[Val Polcevera|Polcevera Valley]] to the northwest and the Bisagno Valley to the northeast. Geologically, it consists of three types of geological formations: the marly limestones of Mount Antola (Carignano and Sarzano areas, as well as the area between Righi and [[Castelletto (Genoa)|Castelletto]] and the Lanterna area), dating from the [[Late Cretaceous]] and [[Paleocene]] periods; the Val Polcevera mudstones (with some outcrops, especially in the Granarolo area), which form the base of the [[flysch]] of the earlier formation; Piccapietra marls (Portoria area and part of the Maddalena and Molo districts), dating from the [[Pliocene]].<ref>A cura di Piera Melli, ''La città ritrovata, Archeologia urbana a Genova 1984–1994'', pag 25 e pag 26, Tormena Editore, 1996, ISBN 88-86017-62-6</ref>

There were several streams and creeks in the area, which over the centuries were covered and/or channeled into the city sewer system to obtain new building areas. Some terms in the city's toponymy refer to these streams, for example in the street at the Ponte Reale (connecting Piazza Banchi to Piazza Caricamento), where the term "''Reale''" would not mean royalty, but would be a deformation of ''rià'' (''rio'', or stream, in [[Genoese dialect|Genoese]]), from the ''riale di Soziglia'' (i.e., Soziglia stream) that flowed in the area.<ref>Riccardo Navone, ''Viaggio nei caruggi. Edicole votive, pietre e portali'', Fratelli Frilli Editori, Genova, 2007 ISBN 978-88-7563-334-9, p. 151</ref> Another example would be Piazza Acquaverde (opposite the [[Genova Piazza Principe railway station|Piazza Principe train station]]), whose name is said to derive from the presence of a pond rich in algae, hence the greenish color, fed by the Sant'Ugo stream (a legend has it that it was [[Ugo Canefri|the saint himself]] who caused the water that fed the pond to gush out).<ref>Riccardo Navone, ''Viaggio nei caruggi. Edicole votive, pietre e portali'', Fratelli Frilli Editori, Genova, 2007 ISBN 978-88-7563-334-9, p. 382</ref>

The historic center is traditionally divided into six areas called ''sestieri'': ([[Prè]], [[Portoria]], [[Molo (Genoa)|Molo]], [[Maddalena (Genoa)|Maddalena]], [[San Vincenzo (Genoa)]], San Teodoro), with the historical trace of the ancient districts of what was once the capital of the [[Republic of Genoa]] being maintained. This subdivision falls outside the one that sees the municipal territory organized into more than a dozen wards (or municipalities): the six ''sestieri'' are currently included in the territory of the ''Municipi I Centro Est'' and ''II Centro Ovest'' (for the ''sestiere'' of San Teodoro alone).

Streets and alleys traditionally were paved with stones or bricks, which composed various designs, from the more linear ones, such as parallel-row or herringbone placement, to more complex ones. The stone slabs were usually of two sizes, a thin and long type (about 12–15 cm by 70–75 cm), called "''cordonini''," and a wider type (24–26 cm by 50–60 com) called "''tacchi''," and sometimes these were alternated with bricks or flanked by cobblestones. In churchyards or palace gardens sometimes the technique of ''risseu'', a [[cobblestone]] [[mosaic]] typical of [[Liguria]], was used.<ref>''Proposta per la riqualificazione di itinerari significativi del centro storico di Genova'', Consorzio Imprenditori Edili Genovesi, 1990, capitolo "Cenni storici"</ref> Over the years, asphalt paving has covered some of the original pavement.

=== Surface ===
In view of the original core's size of 1.13 km² (i.e., 113 hectares, the area of the Prè-Molo-Maddalena neighborhoods),<ref name="pianocivis">[https://web.archive.org/web/20070304084839/https://civis.comune.genova.it/piano_operativo/ Il Piano Operativo per il Centro Storico], sheets [https://web.archive.org/web/20130927224444/https://civis.comune.genova.it/piano_operativo/004_2002.pdf 004_2002 URBAN II: Centro Storico] and [https://web.archive.org/web/20130927224403/https://civis.comune.genova.it/piano_operativo/025_2002.pdf 025_2002 L'edilizia privata in Centro Storico], from the Genoa municipality website</ref> it is cited as the most extensive old town in Europe. In fact, this may be considered an urban legend, as it turns out to be less extensive than, for example,<ref name="civis">[http://civis.comune.genova.it/gabrielli.htm "Il centro storico: da freno a opportunità"] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201126152025/http://civis.comune.genova.it/gabrielli.htm|date=26 novembre 2020}}, insight by Bruno Gabrielli, councillor for urban quality, from the Genoa City Council website</ref> [[Rome]] (1,430 hectares)<ref name="Comune di Roma">[http://www.comune.roma.it/was/repository/ContentManagement/node/N1022151320/Delib.%20n.%2011%20%20ALLEGATI%20%20%20Piano%20Regolatore%20Sociale.pdf "Comune di Roma, Municipio Roma centro storico, Piano regolatore 2008 – 2010"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820123100/http://www.comune.roma.it/was/repository/ContentManagement/node/N1022151320/Delib.%20n.%2011%20%20ALLEGATI%20%20%20Piano%20Regolatore%20Sociale.pdf |date=20 August 2024 }}, from the City of Rome website, p. 10</ref> and [[Naples]] (the latter, with its 1,700 hectares, the largest).<ref name="Napoli 2,0">{{Cite web |url=http://www.comune.napoli.it/flex/cm/pages/ServeBLOB.php/L/IT/IDPagina/11019 |title=Comune di Napoli |access-date=19 August 2024 |archive-date=24 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230924200053/https://www.comune.napoli.it/flex/cm/pages/ServeBLOB.php/L/IT/IDPagina/11019 |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:Genova panorama dall alto.JPG|thumb|Glimpse with part of the historic center, photographed from above the [[Orto Botanico dell'Università di Genova|university's botanical garden]]. On the upper left is the [[Piacentini Tower|Clock Skyscraper]] built in the 1930s to a design by [[Marcello Piacentini]]. In the center of the photo is the bell tower of [[Genoa Cathedral|San Lorenzo Cathedral]] and in the background part of the [[Santa Maria Assunta, Genoa|basilica of Santa Maria Assunta]], the work of Alessi]]

The high density of buildings, especially after the enormous building growth that began with the 18th century, nevertheless makes it one of the historical centers with the highest population density:<ref name=civis /> about 23,000 inhabitants live in the oldest area (also including the port area), distributed in 2305 buildings (value as of 1999) on a volume of about 10 million cubic meters.<ref name="civis"/><ref name=pianocivis />

=== The development of early Genoa and early settlements ===
[[File:Piazza Sarzano Genova 01.jpg|thumb|Sarzano Square, in the [[Molo (Genoa)|Molo ''sestiere'']], one of the first areas of the historic center to be inhabited. This square and its surroundings were also damaged by Allied bombing in World War II and renovated in the following decades. The fountain in the square, the work of [[Bartolomeo Bianco]] and built around the mid-17th century, is located above one of the cisterns that served the city in case of siege. On top of the hexagonal temple that covers the structure is a statue depicting [[Janus]], a reminder of one of the theories that claim the name Genoa derives from that of the Roman deity.<ref>Riccardo Navone, ''Viaggio nei caruggi. Edicole votive, pietre e portali'', Fratelli Frilli Editori, Genova, 2007 ISBN 978-88-7563-334-9, p. 28</ref> With the opening in 2006, after years of construction, of the [[Sarzano/Sant'Agostino (Genoa Metro)|Sarzano-Sant'Agostino subway station]], the square was reached by public transportation for the first time.]]
{{see also|History of Genoa}}

As written earlier, due to the frequent and continuous construction of new buildings on top of what previously existed and after the bombing of the last world war, no Roman or pre-Roman remains are visible. Over the past two centuries, remodeling works in some parts of the city (e.g., [[Via XX Settembre (Genoa)|Via XX Settembre]] and surrounding areas between the 18th and 19th centuries), as well as restoration and extension works on buildings and streets, have repeatedly brought to light numerous ruins and objects related to early city settlements or the later Roman period.<ref name="Bernardini">Enzo Bernardini, ''Liguria'', collana ''itinerari archeologici'', 1981, Newton Compton Editore, p. 168 e sgg.i</ref>

During excavations for the construction of the subway, a 12-meter-long dry-stone wall with nearby remains of hearths and a canal were found in the area adjacent to the [[Genova Brignole railway station|Brignole train station]], the origin of which would date back to a period between the 3rd and 2nd millennia BC. This construction would demonstrate the probable presence of small settlements in the area since the [[Bronze Age]].<ref name="etruschi">[https://ricerca.repubblica.it/repubblica/archivio/repubblica/2008/02/20/gli-etruschi-nel-ventre-della-superba.html Gli etruschi nel ventre della Superba], “La Repubblica” article (Genoa edition), 20 February 2008</ref> A fraction of the wall was later reconstructed and displayed in the subway station that arose in the area, along with another find, namely part of the churchyard of the ancient church of Santa Maria degli Incrociati<ref>[http://www.genovatoday.it/cronaca/metropolitana-genova-brignole-apertura.html Metropolitana Genova, Brignole-De Ferrari: sabato 22 dicembre 2012 apre la tratta], genovatoday.it article, dated 21 December 2012</ref> (a name given to the Hospitallers who had a shelter and church there in the [[late Middle Ages]]).

The presence of the wall (believed after studies to be the retaining wall of a road), as well as the probable remains of a pile-dwelling found during work in the area of the present-day Piazza della Vittoria (the dating of which would date it to a period between 4790 B.C. and 4460 B.C.), led archaeologists of the Superintendence for Archaeological Heritage of Liguria to assume that there was a river port at the nearby mouth of the [[Bisagno (river)|Bisagno]] stream, with a settlement behind it.<ref name="focebisagno">[http://genova.repubblica.it/cronaca/2010/04/03/news/la_superba_nata_in_riva_al_bisagno-3100212/ La Superba è nata in riva al Bisagno "Genova era un porto fluviale"], article from ''La Repubblica'', 3 April 2010</ref><ref>[https://genovaquotidiana.com/2015/12/28/le-palafitte-della-foce-quando-il-piano-casa-non-era-un-problema/ Le palafitte della Foce, quando il “Piano Casa” non era un problema], genovaquotidiana.com article, 28 December 2015</ref>

Reconstructions made by historians in the second half of the 20th century, prior to these findings, had identified the first port area in the area of the "ancient port," about 1.5 km (as the crow flies) west/northwest of this possible river port. There, in the area of the eighteenth-century ''portofranco'' (roughly today's Piazza Cavour), at the time of the first settlements at the base of the Sarzano hill (later named Mandraccio), artifacts were found spread over several layers, the oldest of which dated (through some wooden remains) between the 10th and 9th centuries BC, as well as layers containing artifacts (including many [[amphora]]e) dated as belonging to the centuries between the 6th and 1st centuries B.C.<ref>A cura di Piera Melli, ''La città ritrovata, Archeologia urbana a Genova 1984–1994'', p. 83 e sgg., Tormena Editore, 1996, ISBN 88-86017-62-6</ref> In January 2013, during archaeological inspections carried out along the nearby Spinola Bridge as part of the work related to the expansion of the [[Aquarium of Genoa|Genoa Aquarium]] with a new dolphin tank, remains of vases and amphorae, both Etruscan and Roman, were found, some of them containing fruit stones, legumes and seeds. The finds, recovered at a depth of about 13 meters, would be several hundred meters from what is estimated to have been the coastline in Roman times, leading to speculation that the area was used as a sort of dumping ground by ships.<ref>[http://www.ilsecoloxix.it/p/genova/2013/01/08/APu40ePE-acquario_etruschi_sotto.shtml Resti etruschi sotto l'Acquario] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130111094116/http://www.ilsecoloxix.it/p/genova/2013/01/08/APu40ePE-acquario_etruschi_sotto.shtml|date=11 gennaio 2013}}, article from [[Il Secolo XIX]], dated 8 January 2013, and [http://genova.mentelocale.it/50115-acquario-genova-trovate-anfore-etrusche-romane/ Acquario di Genova: trovate anfore etrusche e romane] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130130025455/http://genova.mentelocale.it/50115-acquario-genova-trovate-anfore-etrusche-romane/|data=30 gennaio 2013}}, mentelocale.it article, dated 8 January 2013</ref>

As for the earliest, more developed settlements, in [[Prehistoric Italy|pre-Roman times]], it is believed that the hill of Sarzano (also known as ''di Castello'' or ''Colle del Castello'', perhaps from the early medieval castle on the site, later to become the convent of San Silvestro),<ref name="Bernardini" /> from which the underlying stretch of sea could be controlled, and its beach, were among the first inhabited places in the center of Genoa. Precisely in order to verify the thesis that saw the Sarzano hill as the site of pre-Roman settlements (specifically a possible boundary wall), the first archaeological excavations carried out explicitly in the area for research purposes were carried out in 1939 by [[Luigi Bernabò Brea]]: the area investigated was the one on which rested part of the (destroyed) church of Santa Maria in Passione, but the results and conclusions reached are not known for sure. More systematic excavations took place in the following decades, facilitated by the work of restoring the area after the bombing suffered during World War II.<ref>Marco Milanese, ''Scavi nell'oppidum preromano di Genova: (Genova, San Silvestro 1) – Volume 1'', collana Studia archaeologica Volume 48, L'Erma di Bretschneider, 1987, ISBN 88-7062-621-0, [https://books.google.com/books?id=Ge0mrXTQVIUC&dq=genova+preromana&pg=PA30 pag 30 e seg]</ref> The findings show that as early as the 6th century B.C. the beach was a point of exchange between merchants from the Mediterranean cities that frequented the port and the inland populations. Excavations on the hill, after bombings had destroyed the convent of San Silvestro, showed that layers as much as four meters thick were present in the area, with ruins, walls and stones used in earlier construction. The construction of dwellings began around the 6th century B.C. and continued until the 2nd century B.C., while around the 4th century B.C. the area was protected with an initial enclosure of drystone walls. The top of the hill was probably flattened, and terracing was built along its sides.<ref>Marco Milanese, ''[http://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/l-italia-preromana-i-siti-liguri-genova_(Il-Mondo-dell'Archeologia)/ L'Italia preromana. I siti liguri: Genova]'', from the [[Enciclopedia Treccani|Treccani Encyclopedia]] website, taken from The World of Archaeology (2004)</ref> Until the recent discoveries in the area of Brignole and the mouth of the Bisagno River, mentioned just above,<ref name="focebisagno" /> which have raised new questions about the location of the first city nucleus, it was believed that the port city of Genoa at that time most likely included the area corresponding roughly to the [[Molo (Genoa)|Molo district]].<ref name="Bernardini" />

Centuries later, the Sarzano hill shows nothing of the original buildings, but highlights the [[Embriaci Tower|Embriaci tower]], the convent of [[Santa Maria di Castello]], and the Campopisano esplanade, a symbol of the naval victory of the [[Republic of Genoa]] over the neighboring Maritime Republic of [[Pisa]].

[[File:Genova-centro storico-IMG 1503.JPG|thumb|left|Sarzano Hill. The [[Embriaci Tower|Embriaci tower]] and the bell tower of the church of [[Santa Maria di Castello]] are visible.]]

Numerous burials, containing urns (cremation was used, as in much of the ancient world) and grave goods, have also been found in the area of the historic center: the aforementioned work on the construction of Via XX Settembre brought to light 73 tombs in the upper part of the street and around [[Piazza De Ferrari]], which with work in the area in the following decades came to 121 (late 1960s). It is estimated that this necropolis had been used between the fifth and third centuries B.C.<ref name="Bernardini" /><ref name="preromana">A cura di Piera Melli, ''La città ritrovata, Archeologia urbana a Genova 1984–1994'', Tormena Editore, 1996, ISBN 88-86017-62-6, p. 33 e sgg.</ref> The tombs, part of which had already been looted or damaged in ancient times, each contained several urns and were, for the most part of those discovered, of a type similar to that used by the [[Etruscan civilization|Etruscans]] of northern Etruria, different from that typical of the Ligurian populations of previous centuries, probably the result of a custom adopted through immigration.<ref name="MelliPreromana74">Piera Melli, ''Genova preromana. Città portuale del Mediterraneo tra il VII e il III secolo a.C.'', Fratelli Frilli Editori, seconda edizione 2008, ISBN 978-88-7563-336-3, pp. 74–75</ref> Historians, based on the characteristics of the tombs found (such as the greater density of them in some areas) and the discovery of the remains of other destroyed burials, believe that those identified are only a small part of those that originally constituted the necropolis.<ref name="MelliPreromana74" /> More recent work related to events hosted by the city has led to the discovery of early medieval burials in Via San Lorenzo<ref>See references in [https://ricerca.repubblica.it/repubblica/archivio/repubblica/2001/03/22/due-scheletri-nel-cantiere.html Due scheletri nel cantiere] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820123627/https://ricerca.repubblica.it/repubblica/archivio/repubblica/2001/03/22/due-scheletri-nel-cantiere.html |date=20 August 2024 }}, article in ''La Repubblica'', Genoa edition, 22 March 2001 and [https://ricerca.repubblica.it/repubblica/archivio/repubblica/2001/06/16/via-lorenzo-la-sfida-culturale.html Via San Lorenzo, la sfida culturale] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820123631/https://ricerca.repubblica.it/repubblica/archivio/repubblica/2001/06/16/via-lorenzo-la-sfida-culturale.html |date=20 August 2024 }}, article in ''La Repubblica'', Genoa edition, 16 June 2001</ref> (in 2001, during road resurfacing work for the Genoa G8) and a burial mound in the Acquasola area (in 2008, during work for the subway). The latter discovery, according to some initial analyses, could refer to settlements temporally preceding the finds found in Castello Hill, thus proving that the first settlements in this area of the city center undergoing works would predate what has been believed so far.<ref name="etruschi" />

While the Etruscans probably traded with local populations even before the 6th century B.C., it was only with the partitioning of areas of influence in the [[Mediterranean Sea]] that occurred after the [[Battle of Alalia]] (c. 540 B.C.) that ancient Genoa came strongly into the sphere of Etruscan political/cultural influence. The result of this interest in the area by the neighboring Etruscan civilization would lead to the enlargement of the settlement on Castello Hill.<ref>Piera Melli, ''Genova preromana. Città portuale del Mediterraneo tra il VII e il III secolo a.C.'', Fratelli Frilli Editori, seconda edizione 2008, ISBN 978-88-7563-336-3, p. 35 e sgg.</ref><ref>Marco Milanese, ''Gli scavi dell'oppidum preromano di Genova'', Volume 1, L'Erma di Bretschneider editore, 1987, ISBN 978-88-7062-621-6, [https://books.google.com/books?id=Ge0mrXTQVIUC&dq=genova%20cippo%20etrusco&pg=PA324 pag 324] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820123633/https://books.google.it/books?id=Ge0mrXTQVIUC&lpg=PA325&ots=8WQ7E5xD1m&dq=genova+cippo+etrusco&hl=it&pg=PA324#v=onepage&q=genova%20cippo%20etrusco&f=false#v=onepage&q&f=false |date=20 August 2024 }}</ref> According to a recent theory, the name "''Genoa''" itself would derive from the Etruscan term "''kainua''" (new city), which probably could have been employed to refer to new settlements.<ref>Piera Melli, ''Genova preromana. Città portuale del Mediterraneo tra il VII e il III secolo a.C.'', Fratelli Frilli Editori, seconda edizione 2008, ISBN 978-88-7563-336-3, p. 18</ref> Finds that can be linked to the Etruscan presence also include a probable [[Boundary marker|boundary stone]], containing the [[Etruscan language|Etruscan-language]] inscription ''mi nemetiés'', identified in the area of the former convent of San Silvestro and dated around the first half of the fifth century B.C.<ref>[[Mauro Cristofani]], ''Dizionario illustrato della civiltà Etrusca'', [[Giunti Editore]], 1985, ISBN 978-88-09-21728-7, [https://books.google.com/books?id=8GS2PecOg2QC&pg=PA123 pag 123] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820123736/https://books.google.it/books?id=8GS2PecOg2QC&pg=PA123&hl=it#v=onepage&q&f=false |date=20 August 2024 }}</ref><ref>Marco Milanese, ''Gli scavi dell'oppidum preromano di Genova'', Volume 1, L'Erma di Bretschneider editore, 1987, ISBN 978-88-7062-621-6, [https://books.google.com/books?id=Ge0mrXTQVIUC&dq=genova%20cippo%20etrusco&pg=PA325 pag 325] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820123740/https://books.google.it/books?id=Ge0mrXTQVIUC&lpg=PA325&ots=8WQ7E5xD1m&dq=genova+cippo+etrusco&hl=it&pg=PA325#v=onepage&q=genova%20cippo%20etrusco&f=false#v=onepage&q&f=false |date=20 August 2024 }}</ref><ref>A cura di Piera Melli, ''La città ritrovata, Archeologia urbana a Genova 1984–1994'', Tormena Editore, 1996, pp. 34 e 35, ISBN 88-86017-62-6</ref>

Adding to the difficulty in reconstructing this period of the city's history, there is also the fact that not even the later Latin sources (at least those that have come down to us) report information on the origin of ''Genua'', but merely mention it in connection with its relations with Rome.<ref>Marco Milanese, ''Scavi nell'oppidum preromano di Genova: (Genova, San Silvestro 1) – Volume 1'', collana Studia archaeologica Volume 48, L'Erma di Bretschneider, 1987, ISBN 88-7062-621-0, [https://books.google.com/books?id=Ge0mrXTQVIUC&dq=genova%20preromana&pg=PA16 p. 16 e sgg.]</ref>

=== The Roman Era ===

In later centuries the city of Genoa would expand into the areas near the hill of Castello, but within the boundaries from present-day [[Great Genoa]], established in 1926, there were then settlements of other Ligurian peoples, as evidenced by the bronze Polcevera tablet from 117 BC. Records of Genoa at the time, however, are not very numerous, with the exception of those that show the city and its inhabitants engaged in the wars of the Romans, often in a position opposite to that of the other Ligurian tribes and towns.

Genoa, like other Ligurian towns, was probably linked to Rome by economic and political motives as early as the 4th century BCE. During the [[Second Punic War]] the city, regarded as ''foedus aequum'' in Roman international politics, was destroyed by General [[Mago Barca]], [[Hannibal]]'s brother, in 205 BC. A few years later the propraetor [[Spurius Lucretius Tricipitinus|Spurius Lucretius]] undertook the reconstruction, probably because of the strategic importance of the city and its port, due to its location that allowed both sea access to the western Mediterranean and land access to the [[Po Valley]].<ref name="romana">A cura di Piera Melli, ''La città ritrovata, Archeologia urbana a Genova 1984–1994'', p. 38 e sgg., Tormena Editore, 1996, ISBN 88-86017-62-6</ref> The new post-reconstruction settlement probably had its center no longer on the hill, but in an intermediate area between it and the port, between the present Via di San Bernardo and Via di Canneto il Lungo, in the Molo ''sestiere''.<ref>Paola Pettinotti, ''Breve storia di Genova. Dalle origini ai giorni nostri'', Coedit Edizioni, 2012, ISBN 978-88-96608-20-3, pag 3 e 4</ref>

The author and traveler Henry Aubert, in his essay Cities and People of Italy (''Villes et gens d'Italie'', published in Paris in 1923), provides a concise portrait of the historic center of a city-''emporium'', defined as nothing more than a marketplace with no political importance. Aubert cannot help but quote the geographer [[Strabo]] when the latter stated how in Genoa nothing was sold but honey, cattle, hides, wine, and oil. Aubert believed that the historic city occupied the same geographical position as the time in which he was writing, between the Lighthouse (not the [[Lighthouse of Genoa|Lanterna]], but the old lighthouse on the pier that illuminated the entrance to the [[Port of Genoa|port]] in antiquity), which dates from Roman times, and the [[Carignano (Genoa)|hill of Carignano]] on one side, the sea and the fort called Castelletto today on the other.

The writer states:

{{blockquote|It included the ''oppidum'', now the Molo district, with its narrow streets (n. : it refers to the ''caruggi'') full of people, the heart and cradle of the city, which foreigners rarely visit, and in which there is at least one beautiful thing: the ancient and unique church of Santa Maria di Castello, which was the first cathedral of Genoa, and where lovers of historical memories can find interesting things (n. : Our Lady was crowned queen of Genoa in 1657); the Neapolis, situated behind the ''Oppidum'', in a gorge where only the connoisseurs and the intrepid curious dare to venture; the ''Statio'', or military city, which later became the residential city, and finally the ''Emporium'', the ''raison d'être'' of all the rest, the active city, of trade and commerce...}}

He concludes:

{{blockquote|This is the most characteristic part of modern Genoa, the part where the medieval life took place, the part that makes it resemble Naples with its intricate, sloping streets and the gray color of its slate roofs...}}

[[File:TabulaPeutingeriana - croppen on Genoa 01.jpg|thumb|upright=1.8|The surroundings of Genoa in the [[Tabula Peutingeriana]], an ancient Roman map showing the military routes of the Empire (here in a copy from the late 19th century). Genoa is marked as a supply station.<ref>Gaetano Poggi, ''[[iarchive:genovapreromanar00pogg|Genova Preromana Romana E Medioevale]]'', Editore Libreria Moderna, 1914, [https://archive.org/stream/genovapreromanar00pogg#page/n95/mode/2up Illustrazione 18]</ref>]]

In the Corvetto Square area, during construction work on some buildings (in the fall of 2011), the remains of a farm from the Roman period (2nd century BC) were found. According to early research there would also be traces of canalization, in which water taken from streams originating from the Righi area flowed, and the terrain would show the presence of terracing.<ref>[http://www.ilsecoloxix.it/p/genova/2011/11/21/AOgFCLPB-corvetto_fattoria_romana.shtml Una fattoria romana a Corvetto] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111124005157/http://www.ilsecoloxix.it/p/genova/2011/11/21/AOgFCLPB-corvetto_fattoria_romana.shtml|date=24 November 2011}}, article from [[Il Secolo XIX]], 21 November 2011</ref>

After the reconstruction the city's port, and consequently the city itself, grew in importance. In 147 B.C. the [[Roman consul]] [[Spurius Postumius Albinus Magnus|Postumius Albinus]] began the construction of the [[Via Postumia]], which connected Genoa with [[Roman Aquileia|Aquileia]], equipped with a river port accessible from the [[Adriatic Sea]].<ref>[http://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/via-postumia_%28Enciclopedia-Italiana%29/ Voce Via Postumia], from the [[Enciclopedia Treccani|Encyclopedia Treccani]], reported on the website of the [[Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana|Italian Encyclopedia Institute]]</ref> Genoa then became, during the reign of [[Julius Caesar|Gaius Julius Caesar]], the most important port in [[Cisalpine Gaul]].<ref>[http://dizionari.repubblica.it/Enciclopedia/G/genova.php Voce Genova] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140514105929/http://dizionari.repubblica.it/Enciclopedia/G/genova.php|data=14 maggio 2014}} In the [[Zanichelli]] Encyclopedia, quoted from the website of ''La Repubblica''</ref>

Finds and research in recent decades suggest that Genoa was crossed by a number of Roman roads, the route of which, however, is not certain and may have changed over time. One of the hypotheses involves the bifurcation of the road coming from the east at the height of the necropolis in the present-day Acquasola area: from there one road would have transited between the hill of Sant'Andrea and the hill of Castello, then reaching the harbor area and skirting the shore, while the second would have taken a more northerly route, through what would become the ''sestieri'' of Portoria and Maddalena, rejoining the former in the latter and continuing towards the west.<ref name=romana />

The city of Genoa is featured in the [[Tabula Peutingeriana]], a medieval reproduction of a Roman map, which showed the main routes of the Empire, and which is believed to have been compiled in later stages, probably starting in the second century B.C. (the [[Via Aemilia Scauri]], built only in 109 B.C., being omitted from it). [[Strabo]] in his [[Geographica]] (book IV, chapter 6), published in its first version a few years before the end of the 1st century BC, calls Genoa "the emporium of the Ligurians." The city is also mentioned as an ''oppidum'' in the list concerning the Ligurian region that [[Pliny the Elder]] compiled in the third chapter of his ''[[Natural History (Pliny)|Naturalis historia]]'', situating it between the Porcifera and Fertor rivers (normally identified with the [[Polcevera]] and [[Bisagno (river)|Bisagno]] streams):<ref name="MelliPreromana74"/>

{{blockquote|Flumen Rutuba, oppidum Album Intimilium, flumen Merula, oppidum Album Ingaunum, portus Vadorum Sabatium, flumen Porcifera, oppidum Genua, fluvius Fertor, portus Delphini, Tigulia intus, Segesta Tiguliorum, flumen Macra, Liguriae finis.|[[Pliny the Elder]], ''[[Natural History (Pliny)|Naturalis historia]]'', Liber III}}

While the construction of the Via Aemilia Scauri cut off the city and the entire coast from direct trade to [[southern France]] (then part of the [[Roman province]] of [[Gallia Narbonensis]]), it had probably prevented the territory from being caught up in the passage of armies in the subsequent civil wars of 49–45 B.C. and 44-31 B.C.<ref>Paola Pettinotti, ''Breve storia di Genova. Dalle origini ai giorni nostri'', Coedit Edizioni, 2012, ISBN 978-88-96608-20-3, pag 4</ref>

A certain regularity in the streets that make up the medieval historic center (roughly comprised between present-day Via San Lorenzo, Via [[Filippo Turati]], Salita Pollaioli and the hill of Castello) and the fact that even the few finds of buildings of Roman origin unearthed in the area seem to have an orientation compatible with this arrangement, has led to the assumption that a military encampment existed in the area, from whose shape the neighborhood would have developed.<ref>Gaetano Poggi, in his ''Genova Preromana Romana E Medioevale'' (1914), speculates instead that a Roman military camp was present in the Soziglia area. Cf. ''[[iarchive:genovapreromanar00pogg|Genova Preromana Romana E Medioevale]]'', Editore Libreria Moderna, 1914, [https://archive.org/stream/genovapreromanar00pogg#page/22/mode/2up chapter 2]</ref> However, there is no firm evidence to support this hypothesis.<ref name="romana" /><ref name="Milanesetreccani">Marco Milanese, ''[http://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/l-italia-preromana-i-siti-liguri-genova_%28Il-Mondo-dell'Archeologia%29/ L'Italia preromana. I siti liguri: Genova]'', in ''Il Mondo dell'Archeologia'', [[Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana]], 2004</ref>
[[File:San Siro Genova 01.jpg|thumb|left|[[Romanesque art|Romanesque]] relief depicting [[Syrus of Genoa|Saint Syrus]] and some heraldic symbols, in Vico San Pietro della Porta]]

The remains of a Roman ''[[domus]]'' were found in the area of today's Matteotti Square (near the Ducal Palace). Excavations in the area, carried out on several occasions since 1975, identified the first use of the area in the final period of the [[Roman Republic]] (1st century B.C.)<ref name=melli2007>Piera Melli, ''[http://www.archeoliguria.beniculturali.it/index.php?it/131/pubblicazioni/15/2007-itinerari-archeologici-a-genova-alla-scoperta-della-citt-che-non-si-vede Itinerari archeologici a Genova. Alla scoperta della città che non si vede] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170222054326/http://www.archeoliguria.beniculturali.it/index.php?it/131/pubblicazioni/15/2007-itinerari-archeologici-a-genova-alla-scoperta-della-citt-che-non-si-vede |date=22 febbraio 2017 }}'', Genova, De Ferrari, 2007, pag 15 e seg</ref> The building, passing through numerous modifications and periods of decay, would remain in use until the 7th century. According to the findings, the area would have undergone heavy modifications in the 12th and 13th centuries, when a cemetery was created connected to the nearby church of St. Ambrose, but by that time the walls that made up the building had probably already collapsed.<ref>A cura di Piera Melli, ''La città ritrovata, Archeologia urbana a Genova 1984–1994'', p. 272 e sgg., Tormena Editore, 1996, ISBN 88-86017-62-6</ref> An epigraph dedicated to [[Fortuna Redux]] was also found in the excavations, probably belonging to some religious building or monument that existed in the area in Roman times.<ref>Alberta Bedocchi, Emanuela Profumo, ''I caruggi di Genova'', [[Newton Compton Editori]], ISBN 978-88-541-0929-2, p. 365</ref> A short distance from the remains of the ''domus'', adjacent to the corner of the church of St. Ambrose, the remains of a water pipe, made (or perhaps simply restored) in the 3rd century,<ref name=melli2007 /> were found during the same excavations. Other finds, from the Republican and even later periods, were made in nearby areas, such as those in 1986 in the area occupied by the [[Santissimo Nome di Maria e degli Angeli Custodi, Genoa|Scuole Pie Church]].<ref name="romanarepubblicana">A cura di Piera Melli, ''La città ritrovata, Archeologia urbana a Genova 1984–1994'', p. 284 e sgg., Tormena Editore, 1996, ISBN 88-86017-62-6</ref>

After the beginning of the Christian era, some legends, taken up by medieval and Renaissance writers such as [[Jacobus de Voragine]] and Agostino Schiaffino, have it that [[Saint Peter|St. Peter]]<ref name="Padovano">Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume primo'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 978-88-6070-021-6, p. 79</ref> and Saints [[Nazarius and Celsus]]<ref>Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume primo'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 978-88-6070-021-6, p. 77</ref> passed through the city during the first century. Another legend has it that [[Saint Lawrence|St. Lawrence]] and [[Pope Sixtus II]] stopped in the city on their way to Spain, being housed in a house located in the area of today's [[Genoa Cathedral|Cathedral of St. Lawrence]], where, after their killing, a chapel and then a church dedicated to the saint would rise.<ref name="viaggio138">Riccardo Navone, ''Viaggio nei caruggi. Edicole votive, pietre e portali'', Fratelli Frilli Editori, Genova, 2007 ISBN 978-88-7563-334-9, p. 138</ref> Based on archaeological findings, a stable Christian community was certainly present in the mid-3rd century and used the very area of St. Lawrence as its burial place (but the cemetery that was present was already used in Roman times),<ref name=viaggio138 /> however, there is no certainty about the identity and exact sequence of the first bishops of the [[Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Genoa|city's diocese]], the best known of whom is [[Syrus of Genoa|St. Syrus]].<ref>Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume primo'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 978-88-6070-021-6, pp. 81–82</ref> By his work, or that of his predecessor Felice, the construction of Genoa's first cathedral, initially dedicated to the [[Apostles in the New Testament|Twelve Apostles]] and from the sixth century to [[San Siro (Genoa)|St. Syrus himself]], would be begun in the area west of the ''civitas''.

=== The early Middle Ages ===
[[File:Via san luca genova 01.jpg|thumb|Via San Luca in the evening at Christmas time. The medieval street (formerly known as ''carrubeo recto'')<ref>Alberta Bedocchi, Emanuela Profumo, ''I caruggi di Genova'', [[Newton Compton Editori]], ISBN 978-88-541-0929-2, p. 524</ref> connected the center of the city (''civitas'') with the area of the [[San Siro (Genoa)|church of San Siro]] (''burgus''), until the 9th century the cathedral of Genoa,<ref name="rollisansiro">{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20060821075058/http://www.irolli.it/chiesa_genova/15/chiesa-di-san-siro.html Chiesa di San Siro]}}, from irolli.it</ref> and had numerous porticoes, which later disappeared in the renovations of the palaces that took place from the 15th century onward.<ref>A cura di Paola Motta, ''Itinerario nel centro storico'', collana ''Guide di Genova, nuova serie'', Sagep editrice, pp. 47, 49</ref> Along the street and in the adjacent areas were the palaces of the Grimaldi and Spinola families.]]

Due to some letters (dated 507 and 511) by which [[Theodoric the Great]] granted the restoration of an old synagogue, there is information about the presence of a Jewish community in the city in the early 6th century.<ref>Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume primo'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 978-88-6070-021-6, p. 98</ref>

In 569 the [[Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Milan|curia of Milan]], ruled by Honoratus Castiglioni, fleeing from the [[List of kings of the Lombards|Lombard king]] [[Alboin]], found refuge in Genoa, where it remained for about 80 years. The curia settled in the area of what is now Piazza Matteotti, building a church there, dedicated to [[Ambrose|St. Ambrose]], patron saint of Milan, which over the centuries became the present Church of Jesus and Saints Ambrose and Andrew.<ref name="articolofrilli">Riccardo Navone, ''[https://web.archive.org/web/20090406034920/http://www.frillieditori.com/books/genovacittantica_storia.htm Genova città antica]'', article from the old Fratelli Frilli Editori website, retrieved from the [[Internet Archive]].</ref>

According to reports two centuries later by [[Paul the Deacon]] in his ''[[History of the Lombards|Historia Langobardorum]]'', at the same time as the descent of the Lombards into Italy, in the 670s, Liguria was struck by a plague, which caused numerous deaths and the abandonment of cities and pastures in the countryside as the inhabitants fled:

{{text and translation
|Huius temporibus in provincia praecipue Liguriae maxima pestilentia exorta est. <nowiki>[...]</nowiki> Nam, ut vulgi rumor habebat, fugientes cladem vitare, relinquebantur domus desertae habitatoribus, solis catulis domum servantibus. Peculia sola remanebant in pascuis, nullo adstante pastore. Cerneres pridem villas seu castra repleta agminibus hominum, postero vero die universis fugientibus cuncta esse in summo silentio.|At that time, a very great plague was spreading, especially in the province of Liguria. <nowiki>[...]</nowiki> Since it was rumored among the people that the only way to avoid the slaughter was to flee, houses were abandoned: devoid of inhabitants, they were guarded only by dogs; even cattle remained only in the pastures, for there were no shepherds left. Villas and castles, which had just been crowded with people, were to be seen the next day in gloomy silence, after everyone had fled.|[[Paul the Deacon]], ''[[Historia Langobardorum]]'', volume 1<ref>Traduzione da Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume primo'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 978-88-6070-021-6, p. 106</ref>}}

Between 641 and 643, the Lombard king [[Rothari]] conquered Liguria and assaulted, among others, the city of Genoa, sacking and burning some areas of it, and probably destroying the walls already present,<ref>Alberta Bedocchi, Emanuela Profumo, ''I caruggi di Genova'', [[Newton Compton Editori]], ISBN 978-88-541-0929-2, pp. 11, 14</ref> about whose actual existence, extent and position in this historical period, however, there is no shared opinion among scholars. According to several historians there were in fact defensive works present, predating those about whose existence there is certainty (due to visible remains or historical documentation), from the time of the earliest pre-Roman settlements, but for none of these fortifications is there certain evidence of their actual existence, eventual location and extent, or their eventual modification over time.<ref>A cura di Piera Melli, ''La città ritrovata, Archeologia urbana a Genova 1984–1994'', p. 42, Tormena Editore, 1996, ISBN 88-86017-62-6</ref>

Following the annexation to the Lombard kingdom, Bishop Forte fled the city, taking shelter with the Pope in Rome, and it would be his successor, [[John the Good (bishop of Milan)|St. John the Good]] (a descendant of a noble family from the Gulf of Paradise),<ref>"''il G. sarebbe nato a Camogli, da una nobile famiglia originaria della valle di Recco''" ", from the [http://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/santo-giovanni_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/ entry on Giovanni Bono], from the [[Dizionario biografico degli italiani|Biographical Dictionary of Italians]], Volume 55 (2001), quoted from the website of the [[Istituto dell'Enciclopedia Italiana|Italian Encyclopedia Institute]]</ref> who brought the seat of the curia of Milan back to the city of origin, although on the date of Forte's departure from Genoa and this relocation there is no unambiguousness in the sources.<ref>In Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume primo'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 978-88-6070-021-6, p. 117, 110 and 111 the sack of Genoa and the subsequent flight of Forte are attested in 643 and the transfer of the curia in 655, with the transport of some relics belonging to the body of St. Syrus to [[Desio]]. According to the [http://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/santo-giovanni_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/ entry on Bishop Giovanni Bono] in the [[Dizionario biografico degli italiani|Biographical Dictionary of Italians]], the succession between Forte and Bono would have occurred “''probably around the year 641, to the episcopal throne after the death of his predecessor Forte'',” with Bono already residing for some time in Milan, where he would have died in 651, although traditional sources would (erroneously) attest his death in 669. The chronotaxy [http://www.chiesadimilano.it/arcivescovo-span-class-caret-aria-hidden-true-span/vescovi-precedenti/vescovi-nella-storia-dal-iii-secolo-ai-giorni-nostri/le-origini-della-chiesa-di-milano-br-anatalo-primo-vescovo-nel-iii-secolo-1.23053 on the website of the Diocese of Milan] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160523030216/http://www.chiesadimilano.it/arcivescovo-span-class-caret-aria-hidden-true-span/vescovi-precedenti/vescovi-nella-storia-dal-iii-secolo-ai-giorni-nostri/le-origini-della-chiesa-di-milano-br-anatalo-primo-vescovo-nel-iii-secolo-1.23053|data=23 maggio 2016}} reports 641 as the date of the passage of the title of bishop between Forte and Bono, without specifying when the curia returned to Milan, while the [https://web.archive.org/web/20150707233533/http://www.chiesadigenova.it/home_page/diocesi/00362156_Storia.html old website of the Diocese of Genoa] merely reported that “''From the middle of the seventh century Saint John Bono returned to the Lombard see.''” Federico Donaver, a Genoese historian, in his ''History of the Republic of Genoa'' (1890) dates the transfer of the curia in 645 by John Bono.</ref>

[[File:Genova-Centro storico-Via della Maddalena-DSCF7479.JPG|thumb|left|Via della Maddalena in the afternoon. The street, the nearby square and the [[Maddalena (Genoa)|''sestiere'' of the same name]] are named after the ancient church of Santa Maria Maddalena, which has been present in the area since before the year 1000. It was not until the 12th century, with the construction of the [[Walls of Genoa|Barbarossa walls]], that the area was included within the defensive walls of the urban area.<ref name="rollimaddalena">{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20060818152723/http://www.irolli.it/chiesa_genova/6/chiesa-di-santa-maria-maddalena.html La chiesa di Santa Maria Maddalena sul sito www.irolli.it]}}</ref>]]

After the destruction of the walls by Rothari, the expansion of ancient Genoa and the need to defend itself from the assaults of enemies, as had been the [[Lombards]] first and the [[Saracen]]s later, would lead, starting a few centuries before the year one thousand, to the construction of [[Walls of Genoa|several walls]], of increasingly wider radius, to protect the built-up area, which in later centuries, when not included in new defense works, would be incorporated by the built-up area itself, demolished or buried to make room for new buildings.

Between 848 and 889 a first new city wall was built, partly with the financial help of the [[Carolingian dynasty|Carolingians]], equipped with four gates (Porta San Pietro, Serravalle, Castri and Soprana gates) and four towers (Castelletto, Luccoli, Castello and Friolente), encompassing an area of about 20 hectares.<ref>Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume primo'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 978-88-6070-021-6, p. 117, 118 e 125</ref> Francesco Maria Accinelli, a Genoese historian of the eighteenth century, reports the expansion of the city wall, with the creation of the four gates, in 925 or, as he reports, according to other sources in 935.<ref>Francesco Maria Accinelli, ''[https://archive.org/stream/compendiodelles01accigoog Compendio delle Storie di Genova dalla sua fondazione al 1750]'', vol 1, [https://archive.org/stream/compendiodelles01accigoog pag 22]</ref><ref>Other sources report the period of construction of the city wall as 862–889, with a later modification and reconstruction of it 925–952. Cf. G.B.Nicolo' Besio, ''Genova il centro storico – Itinerari e camminate'', Valenti editore, 1994</ref> This did not prevent the city from again falling victim, in the following decades, to assaults by Saracen forces, which in 935 managed to reach and sack even the church of San Siro.<ref name=articolofrilli />

In 862 there are sources attesting to the presence of Benedictine monks, reporting to the [[Bobbio Abbey|Abbey of St. Columbanus]] of [[Bobbio]], at the church of San Pietro della Porta (where [[San Pietro in Banchi, Genoa|San Pietro in Banchi]] now stands).<ref>Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume primo'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 978-88-6070-021-6, p. 118 e 121</ref> Later they would be entrusted with the [[Santo Stefano (Genoa)|church of St. Stephen]], also outside the walls, whose construction had been decided by Bishop Theodulf.<ref>Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume primo'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 978-88-6070-021-6, p. 142</ref>

In the third decade of the 10th century, the city was attacked and sacked several times by Saracen pirates (in 930, 934,<ref name=giornalesaraceni /> 935 and 936),<ref name=giornalesaraceni /><ref>Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume primo'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 978-88-6070-021-6, p. 125 and 126</ref> who took numerous prisoners, although the Genoese fleet managed to intercept the Arab ships after the last reprisal, freeing fellow citizens captured during this last attack.<ref name="giornalesaraceni">[https://www.rinodistefano.com/docs/media/Il-Giornale_Genova_18-Apr-2008_Pag52.pdf I pirati saraceni all'assalto di Genova], article in [[Il Giornale]], Genoa edition, 18 April 2008</ref><ref>[[Agostino Giustiniani]], ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=X70O38FhZdwC Annali della repubblica di Genova di Monsignor Giustiniani, Volume 1]'', terza edizione, libraio Canepa, Genova, 1854, [https://books.google.com/books?id=X70O38FhZdwC&pg=PA124 pag 124]</ref> It was precisely the continuous assaults that were among the reasons that, in 985, led the bishop of Genoa to transfer the episcopal see from the church of San Siro (at the time named after the [[Apostles in the New Testament|Twelve Apostles]]), to that of San Lorenzo, inside the then existing walls.<ref>Francesco Maria Accinelli, ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=dgEHAAAAcAAJ&q=mura+di+genova+925+e+il+952 Compendio delle Storie di Genova dalla sua fondazione al 1776] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820124243/https://books.google.it/books?id=dgEHAAAAcAAJ&dq=mura+di+genova+925+e+il+952&hl=it&source=gbs_navlinks_s |date=20 August 2024 }}'', vol 1, [https://books.google.com/books?id=dgEHAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA15 pag 15] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820124250/https://books.google.it/books?id=dgEHAAAAcAAJ&hl=it&pg=PA15#v=onepage&q&f=false |date=20 August 2024 }}</ref>

In the mid-10th century [[Berengar II of Italy|Berengar II of Ivrea]], [[King of Italy]], divided the north into three marches, entrusting the one that included Genoa and eastern Liguria to [[Oberto I]] (Marca Obertenga, later called Marca Januensis). In the struggle between Berengar and [[Otto the Great|Otto of Saxony]], Marquis Oberto sided with the latter, while the city of Genoa swore allegiance to Berengar and his son [[Adalbert of Italy|Adalbert]], thus obtaining a diploma in 958 declaring the city and the possessions of its citizens independent from "''duke, marquis and count, sculdascio, dean or any other great or small person of our kingdom.''"<ref name="rmnapoli">Gina Fasoli e Francesca Bocchi, ''La città medievale italiana'', [http://www.rm.unina.it/didattica/strumenti/fasoli_bocchi/testimonianze/test13.htm 13. Diploma di Berengario e Adalberto ai Genovesi (958)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220416095249/http://www.rm.unina.it/didattica/strumenti/fasoli_bocchi/testimonianze/test13.htm |date=16 April 2022 }}, From the website ''Medieval Networks'' of the [[Università degli Studi di Napoli Federico II|University of Naples Federico II.]]</ref> These concessions allowed the city to officially, though not fully, gain a form of political independence.

Prior to the construction of the city walls in the 12th century (known as the [[Frederick Barbarossa|Barbarossa]] walls, with a perimeter four times as large as the previous ones),<ref name="rolliestradenuove">[http://www.rolliestradenuove.it/html/storia.asp Storia] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090530221750/http://www.rolliestradenuove.it/html/storia.asp|data=30 maggio 2009}}, from the website ''Genova: le Strade Nuove e il Sistema dei Palazzi dei Rolli''</ref> three zones were distinguished in the city: the ''castrum'', i.e., the area of the initial settlement around Sarzano; the ''ripa'' area, where traffic and activities related to the port took place; and finally the ''burgus'', outside the walls, where the first cathedral was located, the [[San Siro (Genoa)|church of San Siro]], which still exists today, although it has been partially destroyed and rebuilt several times.<ref>Teofilo Ossian De Negri, ''Storia di Genova'', [[Giunti Editore]], ISBN 88-09-02932-1, ISBN 978-88-09-02932-3, [https://books.google.com/books?id=2jCNYMnOdXUC&q=Compagna&pg=PA175 p. 176 e sgg.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820124322/https://books.google.it/books?id=2jCNYMnOdXUC&pg=PA175&vq=Compagna&source=gbs_search_s&hl=it#v=onepage&q&f=false#PPA175,M1 |date=20 August 2024 }}</ref> The construction of the walls, in addition to incorporating the peripheral area of the church of San Siro into the city, also included the area (closer to the previous circle of walls) of the Basilica of [[Santa Maria delle Vigne]], which had risen about three centuries earlier in an area called Vigne del Re,<ref>Alberta Bedocchi, Emanuela Profumo, ''I caruggi di Genova'', [[Newton Compton Editori]], ISBN 978-88-541-0929-2, p. 617</ref> a name that would attest to the probable presence of vineyards immediately outside the previous city center. The cultivation of vineyards and the presence of some chestnut groves, would also be confirmed by a document from 886, which describes the area as owned by the monks of St. Peter's Church, the clergymen of St. Syrus Cathedral and the family of the viscount (''vicecomes'') Ydo.<ref>Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume primo'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 978-88-6070-021-6, p. 126</ref>
