{{see also|Albergo (family)}}

This last period of expansion, at the turn of the early and late Middle Ages, saw the first agreements between the city's powers,<ref>Teofilo Ossian De Negri, ''Storia di Genova'', [[Giunti Editore]], ISBN 88-09-02932-1, ISBN 978-88-09-02932-3, [https://books.google.com/books?id=2jCNYMnOdXUC&q=Compagna&pg=PA175 pag 175]</ref> which would give rise to the ''Compagna Communis'' ([[Caffaro di Rustico da Caschifellone|Caffaro]] [[Annales ianuenses|attests its existence]] in 1099, but the precise year of its establishment is unknown), which would in turn be the basis on which the municipality would be born, and the elevation of the [[Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Genoa|diocese of Genoa]] to the rank of metropolitan archdiocese (on 20 March 1133, after Genoa's support for [[Pope Innocent II]] against [[Antipope Anacletus II]]).<ref>Teofilo Ossian De Negri, ''Storia di Genova'', [[Giunti Editore]], ISBN 88-09-02932-1, ISBN 978-88-09-02932-3, [https://books.google.com/books?id=2jCNYMnOdXUC&dq=20+marzo+1133+genova&pg=PA250 pag 250 e seguenti]</ref> The ''compagne'' into which Genoa was divided, corresponding to as many areas of the ancient city, documented as seven in 1130 and eight in 1134, were Castello, Maccagnana, Piazzalunga, San Lorenzo, Della Porta, Soziglia, Pré and Porta Nuova (the eighth added).<ref>Alberta Bedocchi, Emanuela Profumo, ''I caruggi di Genova'', [[Newton Compton Editori]], ISBN 978-88-541-0929-2, p. 33</ref>

Beginning in 1125 the Sottoripa arcades were built, of which, after centuries of modifications, demolitions and reconstructions, a significant section still exists on the edge of Caricamento square and Turati street. The original route of the arcade covered the route from Porta dei Vacca (a few decades after the beginning of the construction of the arcades) to the area of the new pier (today's Piazza Cavour), all within a few meters of the piers.

At that time the area was filled with stores and inns that for a period also occupied the front of the arcades, making them a kind of gallery. Despite the changes that the buildings underwent, on some of the facades, immediately above the arches of the arcade, traces of the old city aqueduct are visible.<ref name="viaggio389">Riccardo Navone, ''Viaggio nei caruggi. Edicole votive, pietre e portali'', Fratelli Frilli Editori, Genova, 2007 ISBN 978-88-7563-334-9, p. 389 e sgg.</ref>

Historian Federico Donaver, in his 1912 ''Le Vie di Genova'', describes the area in medieval times as follows:

{{blockquote|In the Middle Ages, the most glorious expeditions of the Republic left from the port, which was the main landing place. Here were built the ships, the slaughterhouses and the houses of the Embriaci, the Malloni and the Castello.|Federico Donaver, ''Le Vie di Genova – Notizie storiche e curiose ad uso del popolo e delle scuole'', Libreria Editrice Moderna, Genova, 1912<ref name=viegenova>[http://www.viedigenova.com/wiki/Pagina_principale Amateur site] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121231041432/http://www.viedigenova.com/wiki/Pagina_principale |data=31 dicembre 2012 }} in which is reported, exploiting [[MediaWiki]] software, the text now in the public domain of ''Le Vie di Genova – Notizie storiche e curiose ad uso del popolo e delle scuole,'' by Federico Donaver</ref>}}

As already mentioned, [[Diet of Roncaglia|Barbarossa's sights on Italy]] led to the construction of a new defensive wall much larger than the previous one, the construction work on which was begun in 1155 and, after a brief pause, resumed in 1158. After a few centuries, to differentiate them from the later walls, they took the common name of old walls.<ref>Giovanni Battista Canobbio, ''Topografia fisica della città e dei contorni di Genova'', Ponthenier, 1840, [https://books.google.com/books?id=-IwLAAAAYAAJ&dq=mura+barbarossa+1155&pg=PA33 pag 33]</ref>

Initially, not all of the area within the walls was built on, as there were numerous vegetable gardens and land free of buildings owned by the various noble families and monasteries present. It was not until the following century that the urbanization of the city was completed, characterized by a geometrically more regular layout than in the older areas, and with the quarters for artisans and merchants concentrated in the outlying areas.<ref name="cittmedioevale">Jacques Heers, ''La Città nel medioevo in occidente: paesaggi, poteri e conflitti'', Editoriale Jaca Book, 1995, ISBN 978-88-16-40374-1, [https://books.google.com/books?id=sQ8S5St522MC&dq=Santa%20Maria%20degli%20Incrociati&pg=PA212 pag 212 e seg]</ref>

The city was not unaffected by the clashes between [[Guelphs and Ghibellines]] that took place from the 12th century, which intersected with the internal political rivalries of the various noble families (among the Guelph and predominant ones, called ''rampini'', were the Fieschi and Grimaldi families; among the Ghibelline ones, called ''mascherati'', were the Doria and Spinola families)<ref name=articolofrilli /> and with the war against Ghibelline [[Pisa]]. The hostilities, in addition to causing turmoil in the city (fires originating from the clashes heavily damaged the church of San Lorenzo in 1296<ref name="comunesanlorenzo">[https://web.archive.org/web/20111117125640/http://www.turismo.comune.genova.it/spip.php?page=scheda&id_article=183 Page on the cathedral of San Lorenzo], from the old site of the municipality of Genoa</ref> and completely destroyed the [[San Pietro in Banchi, Genoa|church of San Pietro in Banchi]] in 1398),<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20060821075402/http://www.irolli.it/chiesa_genova/16/chiesa-di-san-pietro-in-banchi.html Page on the church of San Pietro in Banchi]}}, from the website irolli.it</ref> would also affect inland and coastal towns under the control of the aforementioned noble families. Fire was one of the recurring threats to the buildings in the historic center: between the beginning of the 12th century and the middle of the 13th century, several districts were severely damaged, if not destroyed, by flames. Among the causes were the high density of buildings and the use of wood (typically chestnut), both for the interiors of houses and to raise existing stone and limestone buildings with new floors.<ref>Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume secondo'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 88-6070-022-1, p. 99</ref>

In 1260 the [[Capitano del popolo|people's captain]] [[Guglielmo Boccanegra]] had the first nucleus of the [[Palazzo San Giorgio]] (visible on the present rear of the palace) built in the harbor area as the seat of the municipality. Two years later, with the deposition of Boccanegra, the seat of the Municipality would be suppressed.<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20060827055105/http://www.irolli.it/da_visitare_a_genova/41/palazzo-san-giorgio.html Palazzo San Giorgio]}}, from irolli.it</ref> On the sides of the palace, the piers ''ponte dei legni'' (later ''ponte della mercanzia'') and ''ponte del pedaggio'' (later ''ponte reale'') would later be built.<ref>[http://www.associazioneclaramaffei.org/claraCMS/articolo.jsp?id=0_0&sub=0&art=10 Il Porto medievale di Genova – prima parte] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110622013705/http://www.associazioneclaramaffei.org/claraCMS/articolo.jsp?id=0_0&sub=0&art=10|data=22 giugno 2011}}, article by Gladis Alicia Pereyra, from the website of the Clara Maffei Cultural Association</ref> With the return of the captains of the people in 1271, the Municipality would be moved to the building that formed the original nucleus of the present [[Doge's Palace, Genoa|Doge's Palace]], then owned by Count Alberto Fieschi of [[Lavagna]]. The [[Fieschi family]] had sought to build a palace in the central area of the city, buying some houses from the [[Doria (family)|Dorias]], buildings that were located between Piazza San Matteo and the Serravalle gate (belonging to the 9th-century walls, located next to the [[Genoa Cathedral|Cathedral of San Lorenzo]]). The municipality would officially acquire the building in 1294 and would further expand and modify it in the following centuries. The title of "Ducal" would be assigned only with the beginning of the republic of [[Doge of Genoa|doges]] in 1339,<ref>[http://www.palazzoducale.genova.it/naviga.asp?pagina=76 Storia di Palazzo Ducale] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081228195437/http://www.palazzoducale.genova.it/naviga.asp?pagina=76|date=28 December 2008}}, from the official website of the Ducal Palace of Genoa</ref> the first of whom would be [[Simone Boccanegra]], great-grandson of the captain of the people Guglielmo<ref>Christopher Kleinhenz, John W. Barker, Gail Geiger, Richard Lansing, ''Medieval Italy: an encyclopedia'', [[Routledge]], 2004, ISBN 0-415-93930-5, ISBN 978-0-415-93930-0, [https://books.google.com/books?id=1piMMqjAf1MC&pg=RA1-PA401 pag 401]</ref> and from a family of wealthy merchants,<ref name=articolofrilli /> called by acclamation to the position by the popular party, in opposition to the patrician party that had ruled the city until then. Among his first decisions was the exile for some of the patrician families (mainly Guelphs) who had opposed him and his supporters and the decision that representatives of noble families historically involved in the struggles between the two factions should be precluded from the dogate. As a result of this reform, new merchant families gained power, the so-called ''Cappellazzi'', but they, too, soon proved to be dedicated to intrigue and violence.<ref name=articolofrilli /> The office, initially planned for life, in fact turned out to be much shorter, both for Boccanegra and his [[List of doges of Genoa|successors]].

[[File:Genova1493.png|thumb|upright=1.6|left|Genoa in the late 15th century in a period woodcut published in [[Hartmann Schedel]]'s [[Nuremberg Chronicle]], published in Nuremberg in 1493. In depictions of the time, the buildings that were the seat of ecclesiastical and civil power were depicted larger than their actual size to highlight their importance.<ref>[http://www.fondazione-oage.org/easynews/newsleggi.asp?newsid=63 Il restauro della cupola del Duomo] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161021004917/http://www.fondazione-oage.org/easynews/newsleggi.asp?newsid=63|date=21 October 2016}}, article by the Foundation Order of PPC Architects of the Province of Genoa on the presentation of the restoration work on the Cathedral of San Lorenzo</ref> The two beacons of access to the port are visible: on the right of the image is the tower of the Greeks, located at the end of the old pier, and, on the left, the tower that overlooked the promontory then located in front of the present district of San Benigno, incorporated into the port area. The tower of the old pier, built in the mid-1820s,<ref>''Cronache della commemorazione del IV centenario Colombiano'', Stabilimento Fratelli Armanino, 1892, [https://books.google.com/books?id=h7Y2AQAAMAAJ&q=%22torre+dei+greci%22+1324]</ref> was reduced to half height in 1575 to allow the placement of a battery to defend the harbor.<ref>A cura di Fiorella Caraceni, "''Il Molo Vecchio''", collana "''Guide di Genova''" n 56, dicembre 1977, pag 6</ref> Demolished in the following centuries and replaced in the first decades of the 19th century by the "lantern," placed at the end of the pier extension built at that time, the lighthouse and end part of the pier in turn were demolished in 1929, to facilitate access to the port for large ships.<ref>[http://www.centrocongressigenova.it/lanterne-memorie-bianco-nero/ Lanterne: memorie in bianco e nero], from the website of the Porto Antico convention center in Genoa.</ref> The present "[[Lighthouse of Genoa|Lighthouse]]" on the other hand, whose construction dates back to 1543, was built on the ruins of the western one, damaged by friendly fire in the 1513 clashes between [[Andrea Doria]] and the French occupiers.]]

During the [[Battle of Meloria (1284)|Battle of Meloria]] in August 1284, the Genoese fleet captured some 9,000 soldiers and sailors of the [[republic of Pisa]], locking them up in an area located in the vicinity of the walls and harbor, which to this day bears the name of the Pisan camp.<ref>Paola Pettinotti, ''Breve storia di Genova. Dalle origini ai giorni nostri'', Coedit Edizioni, 2012, ISBN 978-88-96608-20-3, p. 26</ref> The Pisan Republic did not honor the agreements made after the defeat, and a new Genoese fleet attacked and sacked the [[Porto Pisano|Pisan harbor]] and adjoining areas in August 1290: among the items brought back home were parts of the chain that, for defensive purposes, closed the Tuscan port, broken by the Genoese, and which, divided, were displayed in some of the gates of the walls and in several churches and noble villas. The chains remained in Genoa until the approach of the [[unification of Italy]], when (in 1860), as a sign of appeasement, they were returned to the city of Pisa.<ref>Lucia Tartaglia, ''Sulle tracce dell'altorilievo di Portoria'', from ''In Genova'', no. 2 February 2003, reported from [http://www.francobampi.it/liguria/pezzi/catene/altorilievo.htm Franco Bampi's website] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820125416/http://www.francobampi.it/liguria/pezzi/catene/altorilievo.htm |date=20 August 2024 }}</ref>

In the second half of the 14th century, the [[Albergo (family)|Alberghi]] were created, a union of noble families who shared both spheres of influence in the city's political and commercial life and real estate holdings found in the same areas of Genoa. In the following centuries their existence would be marked by several reforms, the result of infighting between families and the emergence of new powers.<ref>Alberta Bedocchi, Emanuela Profumo, ''I caruggi di Genova'', [[Newton Compton Editori]], ISBN 978-88-541-0929-2, pp. 29–31</ref> In the same period the Republic was involved in the [[war of Chioggia]], against its rival [[Republic of Venice|Venice]], a clash of fluctuating course that, although short-lived (1378–1381), would cost both maritime republics a great deal in terms of resources employed. Several buildings in the historic center incorporated architectural details that were the result of looting during the war, such as the [[Lion of Saint Mark|lions of St. Mark]] found on the side of the church of San Marco al Molo and on the facade of Palazzo Marcantonio Giustiniani, both from [[Istria]]n [[Pula]].

[[File:Genova-Portici di Sottoripa-soffitto.jpg|thumb|Porticoes of Sottoripa, detail of the ceiling of the porticoes. The oldest porticoes date back to the 12th century and were modified several times over the centuries. In the second half of the 19th century Alfredo d'Andrade oversaw the restoration of the porticoes,<ref>''Volume 9 di Guida d'Italia del T.C.I, Liguria'', Touring Editore, 1982, ISBN 8836500099, [https://books.google.com/books?id=sTuwrCII3pkC&dq=Sottoripa+alfredo+d%27andrade&pg=PA97 p. 97] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820125424/https://books.google.it/books?id=sTuwrCII3pkC&pg=PA97&lpg=PA97&dq=Sottoripa+alfredo+d%27andrade&source=bl&ots=DAnSILhufF&sig=fGzZjDURpQFVnmKYmFKEpVGBu5M&hl=it&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwju8cjzxcvPAhWK7BQKHbMkBu0Q6AEIPTAI#v=onepage&q=Sottoripa%20alfredo%20d'andrade&f=false#v=onepage&q&f=false |date=20 August 2024 }}</ref> removing the mezzanines that had been built in the meantime, so as to reproduce the ceilings with their cross vaults and ribs from view.]]

Between the end of the 14th and the 15th centuries, a real red-light district was created in Genoa, in the area where [[Castelletto (Genoa)|Castelletto]] (Monte Albano) is now located, in which prostitution (previously widespread in brothels distributed haphazardly in different parts of the city, not without friction with the ecclesiastical power) was strictly regulated. The taxation from this activity was redeployed almost entirely for maintenance works and the expansion of the port.<ref>Paolo Zerbini, ''Colombo per Genova'', collana ''Genova Dove'', Andrea Proto Editore, p. 127</ref> During this period (on 23 April 1407, to be precise)<ref>Giuseppe Felloni, ''Amministrazione ed etica nella Casa di San Giorgio (1407–1805). Lo statuto del 1568'' ("Administration and ethics in the House of San Giorgio (1407–1805): The statute of 1568"), (Firenze: Leo Olschki Press, 2014) p.3</ref> the [[Bank of Saint George]] was founded, which had its headquarters in the [[Palazzo San Giorgio|palace of the same name]]: created at the behest of the city's French governor [[Jean II Le Maingre]], it would remain in operation for about four centuries, until it was dissolved by [[Napoleon]]. The initial purpose of the institution was to manage the enormous public debt of the republic, unifying the various societies that had previously taken care of it.<ref>{{cite web |access-date=17 June 2009 |archive-date=9 March 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080309175408/http://www.lacasadisangiorgio.it/main.php?do=home |title=La Casa delle Compere e dei Banchi di San Giorgio – Cenni storici |url=http://www.lacasadisangiorgio.it/main.php?do=home}}<!-- auto-translated from Italian by Module:CS1 translator --></ref><ref>[https://www.ilcaffaro.com/bancodisangiorgio.php Banco di San Giorgio] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820125431/https://www.ilcaffaro.com/bancodisangiorgio.php |date=20 August 2024 }}, from ilcaffaro.com</ref> This was a period of crisis for the republic, which would last until the early 16th century, with [[List of doges of Genoa|doges]] often being the expression of foreign powers: first the Milan of the [[Visconti of Milan|Visconti]] and later the [[House of Sforza|Sforza]], and [[France in the Middle Ages|France]]. Foreign control over politics and constant internal struggles, however, did not put a brake on continued building growth and renovation of pre-existing areas, and in Via San Luca, then the main route from the center to the western edge of the city, the palaces of the Spinola, Grimaldi, Pinelli, and Lomellini families were built.<ref name=viegenova />

In 1493 a first group of [[Sephardic Jews]] driven out of Spain arrived in Genoa and were forced to settle in the area of Via del Campo and Piazzetta Fregoso. Jewish immigration to the city in these decades consisted largely of former merchants and traders who, in the new situation prevailing in the [[Iberian Peninsula]] under the reign of [[Ferdinand II of Aragon]], who was adverse to the Jews, had seen much of their wealth disappear in a short time. Almost two centuries later, starting in 1658, this area, near the church of Santa Sabina and part of the [[Prè]] ''sestiere'', would become Genoa's first Jewish ghetto.<ref>Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume quinto'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 978-88-6070-025-4, p. 103.</ref> The collapse of the Genoese population that had occurred a few years earlier due to the plague, with the related demand for new labor and commercial skills, had made it possible for Jews to obtain Genoese citizenship, albeit with severe limitations: with the establishment of the ghetto, the alleys and streets that allowed access to the area were closed off by gates, and among the obligations imposed on the population living there was that of attending masses held in the nearby churches of San Siro and delle Vigne. However, in contrast to what was happening in the same period in other cities located on Italian territory, the constant humiliation and provocation to which the Jewish population was subjected almost never resulted in explicit acts of violence.<ref name="viaggio354">Riccardo Navone, ''Viaggio nei caruggi. Edicole votive, pietre e portali'', Fratelli Frilli Editori, Genova, 2007 ISBN 978-88-7563-334-9, p. 354</ref> This area, popularly still called "the ghetto," is one of the most degraded in the historic center, often in the news for the widespread transsexual prostitution that takes place in its ''caruggi''.<ref>[https://www.corriere.it/cronache/10_febbraio_09/dellacasa_bagnasco_trans_fb2b9a8a-1559-11df-a154-00144f02aabe.shtml Bagnasco, a Genova l'incontro con i trans] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820125935/https://www.corriere.it/cronache/10_febbraio_09/dellacasa_bagnasco_trans_fb2b9a8a-1559-11df-a154-00144f02aabe.shtml |date=20 August 2024 }}, article from [[Corriere della Sera]], 9 February 2010</ref> In the early years of the 21st century, a project to redevelop the area was financed by the municipality.<ref>[http://urbancenter.comune.genova.it/spip.php?rubrique4018 Contratto di Quartiere del Ghetto] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130927171133/http://urbancenter.comune.genova.it/spip.php?rubrique4018|data=27 settembre 2013}}, from the website of the Urban Center of the municipality of Genoa.</ref>

=== From the Renaissance to the end of the Republic of Genoa ===
[[File:Piazza San Matteo, lato nord, Genova.jpg|thumb|In the center is the [[San Matteo (Genoa)|church of San Matteo]], in the 16th-century square of the same name, with part of the Branca Doria palace on the left and the Doria-Danovaro palace on the right. The original church, founded by the [[Doria (family)|Doria family]], dates from 1125, but was heavily modified at first in the late 13th century and then in the mid-16th century. The staircase that gives access to the area in front of the church was built in 1935,<ref>[http://www.diocesi.genova.it/documenti.php?idd=203&parrocchia=153 San Matteo Apostolo ed Evangelista] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928063227/http://www.diocesi.genova.it/documenti.php?idd=203&parrocchia=153|data=28 settembre 2007}}, on the website of the Archdiocese of Genoa</ref> upon completion of some restoration work on the square, in place of the two previous stairways. Several members of the Doria family had their town residences in this area. The typical façade with white (marble) and black (slate) stripes can be seen: the republic of Genoa allowed only four families (the Doria, [[House of Spinola|Spinola]], [[House of Grimaldi|Grimaldi]] and [[Fieschi family|Fieschi]]) to have buildings in which this decoration was present on all floors and not only up to the first.<ref>Riccardo Navone, ''Viaggio nei caruggi. Edicole votive, pietre e portali'', Fratelli Frilli Editori, Genova, 2007 ISBN 978-88-7563-334-9, p. 190</ref>]]

The 16th century, with the rebirth of the Republic of Genoa by [[Andrea Doria]], was a period of strong expansion, known as "''El siglo de los Genoveses''" ("The Century of the Genoese"). Symbolizing this period of growth in the Maddalena ''sestiere'', on behalf of some of the leading noble Genoese families of the time (Spinola, Grimaldi, Lomellini, Pallavicini, Brignole Sale and Lercari), the Strada Nuova, today's [[Via Giuseppe Garibaldi (Genoa)|Via Garibaldi]], about 250 m long, with its stately palaces, was planned and then built, in which, starting in 1576,<ref>[http://www.turismo.comune.genova.it/spip.php?article175 Pagina sui Palazzi dei Rolli] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111117123811/http://www.turismo.comune.genova.it/spip.php?article175|data=17 novembre 2011}}, from the Genoa municipality website</ref> the [[Genoa: Le Strade Nuove and the system of the Palazzi dei Rolli|Rolli]] system was established. The work took about 40 years to complete: from the acquisition of the land in 1551 (construction work would start a few years later, however, in 1558) to the completion of the final paving in 1591.<ref name=rolliestradenuove />

Regarding the construction of Via Garibaldi in place of the pre-existing medieval quarter, a symbol of the strong desire for renewal at that time, Donaver, in his ''Le Vie di Genova'', quoting in turn the 18th-century Francesco Maria Accinelli, wrote:

{{blockquote|Accinelli tells us that between Maddalena and San Francesco di Castelletto and Fonte Moroso there were many notorious shanties, which in 1551 the fathers of the municipality bought for 5000 lire and demolished. The land was sold to more wealthy families who built splendid palaces along a wide street called first "Aurea" and later "Strada nuova". The latter name was kept until a few years ago, when a municipal decree changed it to the name of the Hero of the Two Worlds.|Federico Donaver, ''Le Vie di Genova – Notizie storiche e curiose ad uso del popolo e delle scuole'', Libreria Editrice Moderna, Genova, 1912<ref name=viegenova />}}

Also contributing to this prosperity was the economic link with the [[Habsburg Spain|Spanish crown]], whose investments needed for the wars in which it was involved in Europe were partly financed by Genoese bankers, who could thus enjoy strong income from interest.<ref name=rolliestradenuove /><ref>[http://archiviostorico.corriere.it/2001/gennaio/26/GENOVA_leggenda_della_Repubblica_oro_co_0_010126314.shtml Genova La leggenda della Repubblica d'oro] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820125940/https://archivio.corriere.it/Archivio/interface/landing.html |date=20 August 2024 }}, article from “Il Corriere della Sera,” 26 January 2001</ref>

The construction of the "Strada Nuova" was just one of the works carried out in that period, which saw at work architects such as [[Galeazzo Alessi]] (his works include the [[Santa Maria Assunta, Genoa|Basilica of Santa Maria Assunta in Carignano]], the bell tower and dome of the [[Genoa Cathedral|cathedral of San Lorenzo]] and the design of Porta Siberia)<ref>[http://www.museoluzzati.it/sito/chi-siamo/museo-luzzati-e-porta-siberia Porta Siberia] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170130014215/http://www.museoluzzati.it/sito/chi-siamo/museo-luzzati-e-porta-siberia|data=30 gennaio 2017}}, on the website of the museum dedicated to [[Emanuele Luzzati]]</ref> or sculptors such as [[Taddeo Carlone]] (his works include several portals of the palaces built at the time, such as that of [[Palazzo Doria Spinola|Palazzo Doria-Spinola]]). Also from the same period are the construction of the [[Loggia della Mercanzia (Genova)|Loggia dei Mercanti]] and the [[San Pietro in Banchi, Genoa|church of San Pietro in Banchi]] (on the area occupied by the earlier church of San Pietro della Porta, which was destroyed in 1398) in the Molo district.<ref name=rolliestradenuove /> At the turn of the 16th and 17th centuries, the long and troubled construction of the [[Basilica della Santissima Annunziata del Vastato|basilica of Santissima Annunziata del Vastato]] also took place, begun in 1520 with the covering of the Vastato stream<ref>Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume quarto'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 978-88-6070-024-7, p. 46</ref> and finished only in the mid-17th century.<ref>Claudio Tosi, ''Concilio di Trento, teologia mariana e tradizione francescana negli affreschi della Santissima Annunziata del Vastato'', La Berio n. 2 – July–December 2008, pp. 33–57, reported [https://sites.google.com/site/annunziatadelvastato/home/storia/la-controriforma on the Basilica's official website] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140409234816/https://sites.google.com/site/annunziatadelvastato/home/storia/la-controriforma|date=9 April 2014 }}</ref>

The following century saw the building of a new set of walls, the ''Mura Nuove'' (built between 1626 and 1639), which was not limited like the previous ones to encircling the built-up area because of the need to encompass new areas within it, but provided for the existence of a free space between it and the new route of the walls for mainly defensive purposes. These included the ''Fronti Basse'' on the Bisagno River.<ref name="frontibasse">A cura di Piera Melli, ''La città ritrovata, Archeologia urbana a Genova 1984–1994'', Tormena Editore, 1996, p. 367 ISBN 88-86017-62-6</ref> The construction of the new walls brought the area of the town included within the walls from the 197 hectares of the old walls built until the 16th century to the 903 hectares of the new structure.<ref>Riccardo Dellepiane, ''Mura e fortificazioni di Genova'', Nuova Editrice Genovese, Genova 1984 (ristampato nel 2008, ISBN 978-88-88963-22-8), p. 65</ref>

[[File:Crop on Genoa from Jan Massys of Metsys - Venus van Cythera.jpg|thumb|Detail of ''Venus van Cythera'', by [[Jan Matsys]] (1561), showing a view of the city of Genoa. Part of the [[Villa del Principe|Prince's palace]], built for Admiral [[Andrea Doria]], can be seen in the right foreground, while the dock area is evident in the center of the port arch.]]

In the early 17th century, [[Via Balbi (Genoa)|Via Balbi]] or Balbi street (named after the Genoese noble family of the same name) was also built. Of Via Balbi the first part survives, uphill (about 400 m long), on either side of which stand important and majestic palaces (including the [[Palazzo Reale (Genoa)|Royal Palace]] also known as Palazzo Stefano Balbi), home to several humanities faculties and offices of the [[University of Genoa]] and some museums; a second part, which continued toward Piazza Acquaverde (in the area where the [[Genova Piazza Principe railway station|Genoa-Principe station]] is located, about 315 m long, was demolished in the mid-19th century to allow the passage of the [[Turin–Genoa railway|Turin-Genoa railway]].<ref name=rolliestradenuove/><ref name="stradenuove44">A cura di Paola Motta, ''Le Strade Nuove'', collana ''Guide di Genova, nuova serie'', Sagep editrice, p. 44</ref>

At this time in some buildings in the harbor area, more precisely in the dock area, a mosque was built, which would remain active for about two centuries (from the early 17th century to the end of the 18th century), for the use of the slaves, merchants, artisans and intellectuals of the Islamic religion present in the city. A pillar of the original place of worship can be found in the library of the Faculty of Business and Economics, whose location, as of 1996, is the building resulting from the numerous remodeling that has taken place over the centuries on the volumes of the original building.<ref name=moschea1>{{cite news |date=21 February 2007 |periodical=La Repubblica |title=E dentro la biblioteca di Economia rispunta la moschea medievale |url=https://ricerca.repubblica.it/repubblica/archivio/repubblica/2007/02/21/dentro-la-biblioteca-di-economia-rispunta.html |access-date=19 August 2024 |archive-date=20 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820125941/https://ricerca.repubblica.it/repubblica/archivio/repubblica/2007/02/21/dentro-la-biblioteca-di-economia-rispunta.html |url-status=live }}<!-- auto-translated from Italian by Module:CS1 translator --></ref><ref name=moschea2>{{cite news |date=18 July 2008 |periodical=La Repubblica |title=Un muezzin tra i mattoni rossi quell'antica moschea mai vista |url=https://ricerca.repubblica.it/repubblica/archivio/repubblica/2008/07/18/un-muezzin-tra-mattoni-rossi-quell-antica.html |access-date=19 August 2024 |archive-date=20 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820130032/https://ricerca.repubblica.it/repubblica/archivio/repubblica/2008/07/18/un-muezzin-tra-mattoni-rossi-quell-antica.html |url-status=live }}<!-- auto-translated from Italian by Module:CS1 translator --></ref>

[[File:FeudiImperiali - Genova.jpg|left|upright=1.6|thumb|The surroundings of Genoa in Giovanni Tommaso Borgonio's map (made in 1683 and later updated in 1772). The two walls protecting the town are noted.]]

After its establishment in the 17th century, the Jewish ghetto was also moved for a short time to the vicinity of the port, in the Molo ''sestiere'', and a synagogue was built there in what is now Vico Malatti. From there the ghetto would move, in 1674, to Vico dei Tessitori<ref>{{cite book |author=Aldo Padovano |author2=Felice Volpe |date=2008 |page=133 |publisher=Artemisia Progetti Editoriali |title=La grande storia di Genova |volume=V}}<!-- auto-translated from Italian by Module:CS1 translator --></ref> in an area close to the church of Sant'Agostino and the present-day Piazza delle Erbe, of which no trace remains, however, due to the Allied bombings of World War II, and was then abolished altogether in 1752.<ref name=viaggio354 />

In the ''sestiere'' of Portoria, almost on the opposite side of Via Balbi from the city center, at the turn of the century [[Via Giulia]] was built (based on a 1628 project by patrician Giulio della Torre, hence the name of the street), which took up part of the route of the Felice street (later to become Salita San Matteo) and the Vico del Vento, and allowed to connect the area of Piazza San Matteo (where the Doria family palaces were located) with the Porta degli Archi, located within the circle of the 16th-century walls. Over the following centuries the road would be widened several times and made less steep, until it was replaced by [[Via XX Settembre (Genoa)|Via XX Settembre]] at the end of the 19th century.<ref name="micossi27s">{{cite book |author=Giulio Micossi |date=1966 |location=Genova |pages=27 e seg |publisher=Tolozzi editore |title=I quartieri di Genova antica}}<!-- auto-translated from Italian by Module:CS1 translator --></ref><ref name="giuliaportoria">[http://www.ortidicarignano.it/files/seiitinerariinportoria.pdf I palazzi novecenteschi di via Venti Settembre] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924061908/http://www.ortidicarignano.it/files/seiitinerariinportoria.pdf |date=24 September 2015 }}, from Alfredo Preste, Alessandro Torti, Remo Viazzi, ''Sei itinerari in Portoria'', Grafiche Frassicomo, Genoa, 1997, p. 14 and 15, quoted from ortidicarignano.it</ref>

In 1652, construction began in the area of the little valley of the Carbonara stream, above the church of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, of the Albergo dei Poveri. The construction of the building was overseen, on behalf of the republic, by Emanuele Brignole (who also partly financed its construction in the following years) and Doge [[Oberto Della Torre]]. Construction had to stop almost immediately, in 1656, because of a plague, and the excavations for the foundations were used to bury the corpses of the sick. The church included in the complex, the construction of which began in April 1657, was dedicated to the Immaculate Virgin, in the hope that she would end the contagion. The first part of the building was inaugurated in 1664, but work to bring it to completion continued, with further extensions, for the next two centuries.<ref>Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume quinto'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 978-88-6070-025-4, p. 124 e 125</ref><ref>[https://www.unige.it/comunicazione/documents/AdP_locandina_x_web.pdf L'Albergo dei Poveri rivela i suoi tesori alla città] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161024015545/https://www.unige.it/comunicazione/documents/AdP_locandina_x_web.pdf|data=24 ottobre 2016}}, publication of the University of Genoa</ref>

[[File:Mappa Genova 1766 - clean.jpg|thumb|upright=1.6|Map of Genoa in 1766, published in ''Description des beautés de Génes et de ses environs : ornée de differentes vuës, et de la carte topographique de la ville'', from 1773.<ref>{{cite book |author=Giacomo Brusco |date=1773 |location=Genova |publisher=Ivone Gravier libraio |title=Description des beautés de Génes et de ses environs: ornée de differentes vuës, et de la carte topographique de la ville |url=https://archive.org/details/gri_33125008489805}}<!-- auto-translated from Italian by Module:CS1 translator --></ref>]]

At the end of the seventeenth century, in May 1684 to be precise, Genoa suffered a heavy bombardment by French ships, which caused a great deal of damage in the historic center (depending on the sources, from 8000 to 13000 shells reportedly fell on Genoa, destroying about 3000 buildings).<ref>Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume quinto'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 978-88-6070-025-4, p. 155</ref> Among the buildings that were destroyed and then rebuilt several decades later was also the one where, according to tradition, [[Christopher Columbus]] supposedly lived, located in the area of the Piano di Sant'Andrea.<ref name=colombodove>Paolo Zerbini, ''Colombo per Genova'', collana ''Genova Dove'', Andrea Proto Editore, pag 132</ref><ref name="comuneSoprana">[https://web.archive.org/web/20111117124341/http://www.turismo.comune.genova.it/spip.php?article723&var_recherche=casa%20colombo Casa di Colombo e Porta Soprana], from the old tourism promotion website of the municipality of Genoa</ref> What remains of the rebuilt building (further remodeled in the following centuries) can be seen in Vico dritto di Ponticello.<ref>[http://www.liguriacards.com/genova/vicoponticello/vicoponticello.html Antique postcards] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081223162535/http://www.liguriacards.com/genova/vicoponticello/vicoponticello.html|data=23 dicembre 2008}} of the ''vico dritto di ponticello'' area, predating the changes to the area that occurred at the turn of the 19th and 20th centuries, from liguriacards.com. It shows how the building, in the isolated 21st century, was part of a much denser row of houses, which ran along both sides of the alley.</ref> Initially the city resisted foreign forces and the French ships retreated once they ran out of ammunition, but the following year the Doge [[Francesco Maria Imperiale Lercari]] had to go with some senators to [[Palace of Versailles|Versailles]] to offer the Republic's apologies to the [[Louis XIV|Sun King]]:<ref>Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume quinto'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 978-88-6070-025-4, p. 157</ref> a new phase of decline began for Genoa.

The metamorphoses of the historic center, however, do not stop. Between 1718 and 1724 Domenico Sauli (a descendant of the family that decided to build the [[Santa Maria Assunta, Genoa|Basilica of Santa Maria Assunta]]) financed the construction of the Carignano bridge (named after Blessed [[Eugenia Maria Ravasco|Eugenia Ravasco]]), which, overhanging the area of Via Madre di Dio and Via dei Servi, united, for the first time in a direct way, the hill of Carignano with that of Sarzano.<ref>[http://www.ortidicarignano.it/attivita/genova/ptv/portor21.php Basilica di Santa Maria Assunta e dei Santi Fabiano e Sebastiano] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090518013523/http://www.ortidicarignano.it/attivita/genova/ptv/portor21.php|data=18 maggio 2009}}, from Alfredo Preste, Alessandro Torti, Remo Viazzi, ''Sei itinerari in Portoria'', Grafiche Frassicomo, Genoa, 1997, quoted from ortidicarignano.it</ref> In the second half of the 18th century, the Strada Nuova was extended, with the Strada Nuovissima (today's Via Cairoli) joining the former with the area where the [[Basilica della Santissima Annunziata del Vastato|Basilica of the Santissima Annunziata del Vastato]] is located and from there to Via Balbi.<ref name=rolliestradenuove/> As with the construction of the Strada Nuova, that of the Strada Nuovissima also involved the demolition of the previous building fabric and interrupted the various roads and crosses that connected the underlying area of the ancient ''burgus'' with Castelletto. To this period also dates the demolition of the church of Santa Brigida (on the slope of the same name), demolished to make way for three buildings known as the "Dufour palaces" after the name of the purchaser's household; before this it was used first as a blacksmith's workshop and later as a spinning mill.<ref>{{cite web |title=la demolizione della Chiesa di Santa Brigida |url=https://genova.erasuperba.it/rubriche/storia-di-genova-truogoli-santa-brigida-antico-monastero |access-date=19 August 2024 |archive-date=20 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820130503/https://genova.erasuperba.it/storia-di-genova-truogoli-santa-brigida-antico-monastero |url-status=live }}<!-- auto-translated from Italian by Module:CS1 translator --></ref> Also in the second half of the 18th century, the first system of public lighting was also planned, relating to some of the focal points of the streets in the city center: in 1772 an initial plan was drawn up, which called for the placement of 32 lanterns in as many places, mainly near intersections and squares, but it was not until 25 years later, in 1797, that a first functioning lighting system would be seen to be in place.<ref>Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume sesto'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 88-6070-026-4, p. 108 e 109</ref>

=== The contemporary era and urban expansion of the 19th century ===
With the end of the [[Republic of Genoa|republic]] and the birth of the pro-revolutionary [[Ligurian Republic]] in 1797, many religious buildings (convents, churches, hospitals) were suppressed and nationalized, only to be partially returned to ecclesiastical power in the following decades.<ref name="grandestoria6p141">Aldo Padovano, Felice Volpe, ''La grande storia di Genova – Volume sesto'', Artemisia Progetti Editoriali, 2008, ISBN 88-6070-026-4, p. 141 e sgg.</ref>

[[File:Noack, Alfred (1833-1895) - Genova. Terrazzo di marmo.jpg|thumb|left|''The marble terrace'', in a period photograph by Alfred Noack (1833–1895).]]

Among those that remained in state use and no longer exist is the complex of San Domenico located in the area of today's Piazza De Ferrari (formerly called Piazza San Domenico, taking its name from it): run by the [[Dominican Order|friars of the same name]], who in 1431, starting from the initial church of Sant'Egidio, had expanded it, making it the largest religious building in the city and dedicating it to the saint. After the enactment of laws suppressing religious orders it was first used as a warehouse and prison and then demolished during the construction of the [[Teatro Carlo Felice|Carlo Felice Theater]].<ref>Alberta Bedocchi, Emanuela Profumo, ''I caruggi di Genova'', [[Newton Compton Editori]], ISBN 978-88-541-0929-2, p. 185</ref>

[[File:Mappa Genova 1846.jpg|thumb|upright=1.6|Map of Genoa from 1846, included in the guidebook ''Manuale del forestiere per la città di Genova'' published in the same year by publisher G. Grondona and printer Ferrando.<ref>[https://archive.org/details/guidadigenov0cava Manuale del forestiere per la città di Genova], Editore G. Grondona, 1846, Tipografia Ferrando, litografia Armanino</ref>]]

Another notable religious complex was the convent of Sant'Andrea, in the area of the same name, a [[Benedictines|Benedictine]] monastery that was assigned in 1798 to the [[Piarists|Scolopi fathers]], and later (1810) was deconsecrated and turned into the city jail. Its acquisition and subsequent demolition, to make way for the modernization of the area with the building of the upper part of [[Via XX Settembre (Genoa)|Via XX Settembre]], saw almost 30 years of bargaining (it was begun in 1876) between state and municipal institutions and the construction company, and only in 1904 was it finally torn down. The [[cloister]] of the convent, saved at the behest of architect and archaeologist Alfredo D'Andrade, was rebuilt in the area in 1922 and can be seen in the area between the Columbus house and the towers of Porta Soprana.<ref>Alberta Bedocchi, Emanuela Profumo, ''I caruggi di Genova'', [[Newton Compton Editori]], ISBN 978-88-541-0929-2, pag 467</ref><ref>Anna Maria Nicoletti, "Via XX Settembre a Genova", Sagep editrice, Genova 1993, ISBN 88-7058-507-7, p. 107 e sgg.</ref>

In 1815, with the [[Congress of Vienna]], the Republic of Genoa was not reconstituted, and its territory became part of the [[Kingdom of Sardinia (1720–1861)|Kingdom of Sardinia]].

In the early 19th century [[Carlo Barabino]] presented numerous projects for the urban renewal of the city. Among his works is the central Acquasola Park (1825), in the space of the esplanade of the same name, on the land where the fourteenth- and sixteenth-century walls stood.

The areas had been used for several centuries, first as a dumping ground for the construction work on the Via Nuova (the area was in fact called ''i Müggi'' from the [[Genoese dialect]] for ''the piles'', ''the heaps''), then as a mass grave for the dead of the 17th-century plague.<ref>[https://ricerca.repubblica.it/repubblica/archivio/repubblica/2006/03/16/speleologi-nel-ventre-di-genova-tra-ossa.html Speleologi nel ventre di Genova 'Tra ossa e teschi la nostra Storia'] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820130458/https://ricerca.repubblica.it/repubblica/archivio/repubblica/2006/03/16/speleologi-nel-ventre-di-genova-tra-ossa.html |date=20 August 2024 }}, article from La Repubblica, 16 March 2006</ref> Barabino connected the park with that of the villa, belonging to Marquis Gian Carlo Di Negro, carved out on the area where the 16th-century bastion of Luccoli stood, passing through what is now Piazza Luigi Emanuele Corvetto.<ref name=Manganelli>Carla Manganelli, [http://www.urbancenter.comune.genova.it/sites/default/files/IL%20PARCO_0.pdf Il parco dell'Acquasola] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820130500/http://www.urbancenter.comune.genova.it/sites/default/files/IL%20PARCO_0.pdf |date=20 August 2024 }}, in A. Del Lucchese, P. Melli (a cura di), Archeologia Metropolitana – piazza Brignole e Acquasola, De Ferrari Editore, Genova, 2010, pp.40–42</ref> Part of the park would be demolished a few years later, in 1877, precisely for the creation of the area of Piazza Corvetto and Via Assarotti.<ref name=Manganelli />

[[File:Genoa 1886 - Italy handbook for travellers.jpg|thumb|upright=1.6|Map of Genoa in the 1880s, taken from the seventh edition of ''Italy, handbook for travelers'', published in 1886.<ref>Seventh edition of ''[https://archive.org/stream/italyhandbook01karl#page/n155/mode/1up Italy, handbook for travellers]'', published in 1886, first edition by Karl Baedeker (1801–1859), cartography by Jahre H. Wagner and E. Debes</ref> The main differences from the 1846 map are, in the upper part, the presence of the [[Genova Piazza Principe railway station|Principe railway station]] (called the western station), the presence of the streets and the first buildings that would form the ring road upstream and the neighborhoods connected to it, while in the lower right corner the first buildings of what would become the Carignano neighborhood are noted. The small marine inlet, known as Seno di Giano, immediately below the oratory of Sant'Antonio Abate, where there was the characteristic Campana rock visible in earlier maps, was no longer extant.]]

In 1835, after several changes of opinion on how to reshape the area and related plans proposed to the authorities, the Marble Terraces were built in the area of the old port, designed by architect Ignazio Gardella senior, a kind of promenade more than 400 meters long, which allowed to observe the port and the area behind it from an elevated position. Below the promenade the building housed several commercial premises. The terraces partly replaced the ''Muragliette'' of the 16th-century walls. Their construction, divided into two sections, lasted 12 years, but their existence was very short, as the needs of the port led to their demolition, which took place in five stages between 1883 and 1886, to make room for the tracks used to transport the goods handled in the piers. The short life of the construction had always left much uncertainty about the structure and the area actually occupied by it, but excavations carried out for the restyling of the Old Port area during the [[Genoa Expo '92]] brought to light some of its remains and traces of the foundations, which helped confirm its actual location.<ref name="porto">Catalogo della mostra ''Nuove Opere del porto vecchio, La costruzione del porto di Genova tra otto e novecento'', Sagep, 1987, p. 56 e sgg.</ref><ref>A cura di Piera Melli, ''La città ritrovata, Archeologia urbana a Genova 1984–1994'', Tormena Editore, 1996, pp. 122–124 ISBN 88-86017-62-6</ref> A century would have to pass before new plans for the rehabilitation of the Old Port area would again hypothesize (and later realize) the presence of a promenade along the port arch. The works that led to the demolition of the terraces were part of the great revolution that affected the harbor arch between the mid-19th and early 20th centuries, including the arrival of the railroad near the old pier, the construction of canopies on the harbor bridges to shelter waiting goods from the bad weather, and the replacement of these with reinforced concrete structures after a few decades (the ''Magazzini del Cotone'', after the Genoa Expo '92 used as a cinema and convention center, is among the latter).<ref>Catalogo della mostra ''Nuove Opere del porto vecchio, La costruzione del porto di Genova tra otto e novecento'', Sagep, 1987, pp. 64–65</ref>

In April 1849, a few days after the armistice of Vignale, the people of Genoa, partly because they had not completely abandoned their republican and independence ideas, and partly out of fear of the arrival of the Austrian army as a consequence of the armistice itself, [[Revolt of Genoa|rose up against the Savoy government]], driving out the royal guard and carabinieri present in the city. General [[Alfonso Ferrero La Marmora|Alfonso La Marmora]], sent by the newly reigning [[Victor Emmanuel II]] to quell the uprising, ordered a naval bombardment, which mainly hit the Portoria district (severely damaging the Pammatone hospital) and the port, which was followed by a bloody intervention by the [[bersaglieri]], who indulged in destruction and gratuitous violence against the population.<ref>[http://www.francobampi.it/liguria/sacco/cronologia_sacco.htm Cronologia dettagliata del Sacco di Genova] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091221184207/http://www.francobampi.it/liguria/sacco/cronologia_sacco.htm |date=21 December 2009 }}, from Franco Bampi's website</ref><ref>[http://www.francobampi.it/liguria/sacco/cronologia/bombe_sacco.htm Estratto da] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820130504/http://www.francobampi.it/liguria/sacco/cronologia/bombe_sacco.htm |date=20 August 2024 }} ''I moti genovesi del '49'', Erga, Genova, 1967, reported from Franco Bampi's website</ref>

At the turn of the century the [[Turin–Genoa railway|Turin-Genoa railway]] was built, which would reach the western edge of the city with the Piazza Principe station in 1854.<ref>[http://www.grandistazioni.it/cms/v/index.jsp?vgnextoid=dc7f82ddfc09a110VgnVCM1000003f16f90aRCRD Scheda di Genova Brignole] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120224134037/http://www.grandistazioni.it/cms/v/index.jsp?vgnextoid=dc7f82ddfc09a110VgnVCM1000003f16f90aRCRD|data=24 febbraio 2012}}, from the official website of [[Grandi Stazioni]]</ref> In the area where the initial station arose, built in a temporary building, the first permanent passenger building (by Alessandro Mazzucchetti, 1860)<ref name="schedaprincipe">[http://www.grandistazioni.it/cms/v/index.jsp?vgnextoid=6cc307c09d09a110VgnVCM1000003f16f90aRCRD Scheda di Genova Piazza Principe] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120820075045/http://www.grandistazioni.it/cms/v/index.jsp?vgnextoid=6cc307c09d09a110VgnVCM1000003f16f90aRCRD|data=20 agosto 2012}}, from the official website of [[Grandi Stazioni]]</ref> and its extension (by Giacomo Radini Tedeschi, 1900),<ref name=schedaprincipe /> there were previously the upper part of Via Balbi,<ref name=stradenuove44 /> a barracks (made in the former grain warehouses, dating back to the 17th century)<ref>A cura di Paola Motta, ''Le Strade Nuove'', collana ''Guide di Genova, nuova serie'', Sagep editrice, p. 47 e 48</ref> and part of the 16th-century walls, including the San Michele bastion and the church of the same name.

In 1855, the first Italian Commodity Exchange was established in the [[Loggia della Mercanzia (Genova)|Loggia dei Mercanti in Piazza Banchi]], established through a decree by the head of the government [[Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour|Cavour]], demonstrating the city's continued importance in the economic/mercantile field.<ref name="touring58">{{cite book |access-date=15 June 2023 |date=2001 |first=Touring club |language=it |last=italiano |publisher=Touring Editore |title=Liguria: Genova, le valli, i borghi interni, l'Alta Via dei Monti Liguri, le Riviere di Levante e Ponente |isbn=978-88-365-1871-5 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Nn5Pn0sna3EC&dq=loggia+dei+mercanti+genova+prima+borsa&pg=PA58 |archive-date=20 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820130506/https://books.google.com/books?id=Nn5Pn0sna3EC&dq=loggia+dei+mercanti+genova+prima+borsa&pg=PA58#v=onepage&q&f=false |url-status=live }}<!-- auto-translated from Italian by Module:CS1 translator --></ref><ref>Alberta Bedocchi, Emanuela Profumo, ''I caruggi di Genova'', [[Newton Compton Editori]], ISBN 978-88-541-0929-2, p. 82</ref><ref name="cameracomm">[https://web.archive.org/web/20150618203046/http://www.ge.camcom.gov.it/IT/Page/t01/view_html?idp=483 La Borsa a Genova prima del 1912], article from the Genoa Chamber of Commerce website</ref>

In the 1860s, a reorganization of the city's toponymy was also decided, by Giuseppe Banchero, an operation that led to the cataloguing of some 900 streets. The result of the work was the renaming of 32 streets and the introduction of 86 new toponyms, in some cases relating to newly established streets, in others relating to streets and roads without an official name.<ref>Alberta Bedocchi, Emanuela Profumo, ''I caruggi di Genova'', [[Newton Compton Editori]], ISBN 978-88-541-0929-2, pp. 9–10</ref> Part of the new names introduced referred to domains owned in past centuries by the Republic of Genoa or to battles won by its army.

[[File:Noack, Alfred (1833-1895) - Genova - Strada di Carignano.jpg|thumb|left|Via Madre di Dio in the late 19th century, overlooked by the Carignano Bridge, in a period photograph by Alfred Noack (1833–1895). This area is no longer extant, as many of its buildings were demolished in the 1960s to make way for the Centro dei Liguri executive complex.]]

Slightly more recent than the terraces is the Mazzini Gallery, built in [[Art Nouveau]] style in 1873, in the space obtained by the earthworks of part of the Piccapietra hill and the demolition of pre-existing buildings (including the convents of San Sebastiano and San Giuseppe and the oratory of the Casaccia di San Giacomo delle Fucine).<ref>[https://www.ortidicarignano.it/files/seiitinerariinportoria.pdf Galleria Mazzini] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820130510/https://www.ortidicarignano.it/files/seiitinerariinportoria.pdf |date=20 August 2024 }}, from Alfredo Preste, Alessandro Torti, Remo Viazzi, ''Sei itinerari in Portoria'', Grafiche Frassicomo, Genoa, 1997, quoted from ortidicarignano.it</ref> Since the 1920s, the gallery has hosted the Genoa Book Fair.

In general, in the century between the first decades of the 19th and the beginning of the 20th century, what was then the city of Genoa (especially the ''sestieri'' of Portoria and San Vincenzo) underwent a major transformation, which involved the demolition of many of the old buildings, with the building of Via Assarotti (1850–1856) and Via Fieschi (1865–1870) first and [[Via XX Settembre (Genoa)|Via XX Settembre]] (1892–1912) and Piazza Dante (1930s) later.

This expansion also led to the construction of numerous buildings in the area, overlooking the historic center, that corresponds to the [[Castelletto (Genoa)|Castelletto district]] and the construction of the two ring roads,<ref>[http://www.polis.unige.it/rco/rapu/pagine/schede/scheda%206.htm Piano regolatore edilizio e di ampliamento tra Spianata Castelletto e piazza Acquaverde, 1868] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050331094307/http://www.polis.unige.it/rco/rapu/pagine/schede/scheda%206.htm|date=31 marzo 2005}}, [http://www.polis.unige.it/rco/rapu/pagine/schede/scheda%207.htm Piano per la strada di circonvallazione a mare, 1869] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050331083258/http://www.polis.unige.it/rco/rapu/pagine/schede/scheda%207.htm|date=31 marzo 2005}} e [http://www.polis.unige.it/rco/rapu/pagine/schede/scheda%2012.htm Variante al piano per la sistemazione di piazza Cavour, 1890] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170917213701/http://www.polis.unige.it/rco/rapu/pagine/schede/scheda%2012.htm|date=17 settembre 2017}} from the Polis Department website of the University of Genoa.</ref> which effectively encircle it. Among the main works of this period, in addition to those already mentioned, include the construction of Via Carlo Felice (later to become Via XXV Aprile), in 1825, the building of the [[Teatro Carlo Felice|theater of the same name]], between 1826 and 1828, designed by [[Carlo Barabino]] (the building at that time was damaged and rendered unserviceable by the bombing of World War II, the existing one dates back to 1991), the construction of the first part of the Carlo Alberto carriageway (later to become Via Antonio Gramsci) in 1835,<ref>A cura di Paola Motta, ''Itinerario nel centro storico'', collana ''Guide di Genova, nuova serie'', Sagep editrice, p. 63</ref> of Piazza and Via San Lorenzo (initially the second part of the Carlo Alberto carriageway), built over a twenty-year period starting in 1835, which also involved the dismantling and reconstruction of the facades of some old buildings in the area,<ref name="sanlorenzog8">Alessandro Ombrina, Roberto Ombrina e Paolo De Lorenzi, ''[http://www.studiombrina.com/doc/san_lorenzo_g8.pdf Via San Lorenzo per il G8] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820130514/http://www.studiombrina.com/doc/san_lorenzo_g8.pdf |date=20 August 2024 }}'', from the website of the Ombrina Technical Associate Firm.</ref><ref name="Motta72">A cura di Paola Motta, ''Itinerario nel centro storico'', collana ''Guide di Genova, nuova serie'', Sagep editrice, p. 72</ref> of Via Vittorio Emanuele II (later to become Via Filippo Turati) with the demolition of the old medieval arcade replaced by a larger one in 19th-century style,<ref>Riccardo Navone, ''Viaggio nei caruggi. Edicole votive, pietre e portali'', Fratelli Frilli Editori, Genova, 2007 ISBN 978-88-7563-334-9, p. 410</ref> of the palace of the [[Accademia Ligustica di Belle Arti|Ligustian Academy of Fine Arts]] (built between 1826 and 1831), and finally Piazza Corvetto built at the behest of the mayor and Baron Andrea Podestà in the 1880s,<ref>Alberta Bedocchi, Emanuela Profumo, ''I caruggi di Genova'', [[Newton Compton Editori]], ISBN 978-88-541-0929-2, p. 177</ref> where the monument dedicated to [[Giuseppe Mazzini]] (by Pietro Costa, made in 1882) and the underlying statue dedicated to [[Victor Emmanuel II]] (by [[Francesco Barzaghi]], made in 1886) were placed.<ref>[http://www.museidigenova.it/spip.php?article668 Italia Unita. I capolavori dell'Ottocento – Percorso 4 Dimore altoborghesi e monumenti a Genova nei decenni unitari] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518095209/http://www.museidigenova.it/spip.php?article668|data=18 maggio 2015}}, from the Genoa Museums website</ref>

These operations, often presented as necessary for reasons of hygiene and public utility, as well as for the modernization of the city, were not always welcomed by the population, which protested against the expropriations necessary for the works. Both the city's politicians and the press of the time made the opinions of the builders and the landowning citizens their own from time to time, livening up the political debate of the time.<ref>Anna Maria Nicoletti, "Via XX Settembre a Genova", SAGEP, Genova 1993, ISBN 88-7058-507-7, chapter one</ref> Alfredo D'Andrade, an architect and archaeologist, first director of the Regional Office for the Preservation of Monuments of Piedmont and Liguria and later also representative of the [[Ministry of Education, University and Research|Ministry of Education]] in the negotiations concerning the sale of the prisons (former Benedictine monastery) present on the hill of Sant'Andrea, for the subsequent demolition of the same, in his communications with the central government accused the City of Genoa and the private individuals interested in the construction of being driven by speculative motives, rather than by real reasons of hygiene and public utility.<ref>Anna Maria Nicoletti, "Via XX Settembre a Genova", SAGEP, Genova 1993, ISBN 88-7058-507-7, p. 108/109, text and footnotes 54 and 55</ref>

[[File:Ciappei, Francesco (attivo 1857-1887) - n. 11 - Genova - Veduta da Castelletto.jpg|thumb|View of Genoa and its harbor in the second half of the 19th century, in a photograph by Francesco Ciappei (1857–1887)]]

The walls of the ''Fronti basse'' in 1889 were also partly demolished and used as a retaining wall for an embankment, destined to host in 1892 the exhibition and events for the fourth centenary of the discovery of America. Their presence, moreover, was perceived as an obstacle to the city's expansion to the east (the neighboring municipality of [[Albaro|San Francesco d'Albaro]] had been annexed to Genoa, along with five others, in 1874).<ref name=frontibasse /> The same area where Via XX Settembre was built would become the new hub of city life in the 20th century, destining the other areas of the old city center to decades of progressive decay and abandonment.<ref name=porto /> In fact, in the second half of the 19th century, there began to be a gradual abandonment of the old historic center by families living there (or residing along the "new streets"), who moved either to the new neighborhoods (located in the hillside areas or in the aforementioned raised areas) or to the then neighboring municipalities, while maintaining their work activities in the center; it was precisely this emigration that was to be, along with a cholera epidemic that had hit the city, one of the causes of the decline in the municipality's resident population between the first general census of 1861 and the next one in 1871.<ref name=ottocentogenovese /> The abandonment by the households traditionally residing in the area, especially those with belonging to the upper-middle classes, would continue in the following decades, causing the progressive deterioration of the condition of many buildings, left for years without regular maintenance, and transforming large parts of the historic center into residential areas intended for the poorest segments of the population, such as the elderly or immigrant families from southern Italy in search of work.<ref>Laura Longoni, ''Come parlano i luoghi: viaggio attraverso il centro storico'', in a cura di Laura Bovone, Antonietta Mazzette, Giancarlo Rovati, ''Effervescenze urbane: quartieri creativi a Milano, Genova e Sassari'', [[FrancoAngeli]], 2005, ISBN 9788846466136, [https://books.google.com/books?id=VCuOaUCEqykC&pg=PA105 pag 105 e seg] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820131023/https://books.google.it/books?id=VCuOaUCEqykC&lpg=PA105&hl=it&pg=PA105#v=onepage&q&f=false |date=20 August 2024 }}</ref>

As mentioned initially, it was during this period of major constructions, both public and private, whose works began to unearth the remains of the oldest city and destroy part of the medieval one, that historians began, albeit amid many difficulties and several missteps, to make the first attempts at non-legendary reconstructions of Genoa's origin and the location of its first settlements.

=== From the 20th century to the present ===
[[File:Genoa 1906 - Italy handbook for travellers.jpg|thumb|upright=1.6|Map of Genoa in the early 20th century, taken from the thirteenth edition of ''Italy, handbook for travelers'', published in 1906.<ref>From the thirteenth edition of ''[https://archive.org/stream/italyhandbookfor01karl#page/n157/mode/1up Italy, handbook for travellers]'', published in 1906, first edition by Karl Baedeker (1801–1859), cartography by Jahre H. Wagner and E. Debes</ref> Compared with the 1886 map, one notices the presence of [[Via XX Settembre (Genoa)|Via XX Settembre]] instead of Via Giulia, the transformation of the walls and part of the Bisagno riverbed into the [[place-of-arms]] (where Piazza della Vittoria would later be built) and Piazza Verdi, the demolition of the buildings placed on the Piano di Sant'Andrea, and the fills for the expansion of the port behind the old pier and at the base of the Grazie walls. The [[Genova Brignole railway station|Brignole railway station]], called ''Stazione Orientale'', is also larger and closer to the Bisagno riverbed than the first station built there (in 1868).]]

{{blockquote|Via del Campo, there’s a whore<br />with great big leaf-colored eyes.<br />If the desire to love her comes to you,<br />it’s enough to just take her by the hand.|[[Fabrizio De André]], Via del Campo}}

In 1907 a Department of Fine Arts, the first of its kind in Italy, was established by the municipality, initially headed by historian and archaeologist Gaetano Poggi, former mayor of [[Arquata Scrivia]] between 1890 and 1895 and a member of an earlier commission that was to assess which Genoese buildings and monuments should be subject to special protection because of their historical value.<ref>[http://www.alessandrianews.it/societa/l-ex-sindaco-gaetano-poggi-onorificenze-esposte-biblioteca-143003.html L'ex sindaco Gaetano Poggi e le onorificenze esposte in biblioteca] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170211054820/http://www.alessandrianews.it/societa/l-ex-sindaco-gaetano-poggi-onorificenze-esposte-biblioteca-143003.html|data=11 febbraio 2017}}, alessandrianews.it article, dated 9 February 2017</ref><ref name="sventramento">Lucina Napoleone, ''Genova anni Trenta: i progetti di sventramento del centro storico e l'azione dell'Ufficio di Belle Arti del Comune'', in ''Architettura e città Problemi di conservazione e valorizzazione", Atti Convegno La Spezia 27/28 novembre 2015, ISBN 978-88-98743-57-5, [https://books.google.com/books?id=ofMOCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA105 pag 105 e seg] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820131026/https://books.google.it/books?id=ofMOCwAAQBAJ&lpg=PA107&ots=smCab5VGam&hl=it&pg=PA105#v=onepage&q&f=false |date=20 August 2024 }}''</ref> The new council and the Superintendence of Fine Arts, in the following years, would initiate a series of restorations aimed at bringing back to view the characteristic medieval structures of the walls of some of the buildings in the historic center that had been modified, covered, and re-plastered during the Renaissance, with the aim of enhancing the older aspects of the buildings in the area.<ref name=sventramento />

The construction of Via XX Settembre and the surrounding areas would end in the 1910s, but this would be only the first of many building interventions that would affect the historic center during that century. In the space obtained from the demolition and silting up of the ''Fronti Basse'' on the Bisagno during the 1892 Italian-American Exposition, a space that in the following years had hosted numerous events (including the 1914 Hygiene, Marine and Colonial Exposition), between the 1920s and the 1930s Piazza della Vittoria was built to a design by [[Marcello Piacentini]], with its ''[[Arco della Vittoria]]'' (inaugurated in 1931). Also based on Piacentini's design, the ''[[Piacentini Tower|Grattacielo dell'Orologio]]'' (Clock Skyscraper) was built in Piazza Dante, inaugurated in 1940, which, with its 108 m distributed over 31 floors, was for a long time the tallest building in the city (surpassed by the [[Matitone]] of San Benigno in 1992, by only one meter, but with fewer floors).<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20040908232857/http://www.emporis.com/en/wm/ci/bu/?id=100690 Edifici di Genova]}}, from Emporis.com</ref>

In 1926, by Royal Decree-Law No. 74 of 14 January 1926 and subsequent Royal Decree-Law No. 662 of 15 April 1926, [[Great Genoa]] was created, uniting 19 other previously independent municipalities with the then municipality of Genoa.<ref>[http://www.francobampi.it/genova/territorio/quartieri/index.htm I quartieri genovesi: come Genova è diventata quella che è] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820131103/http://www.francobampi.it/genova/territorio/quartieri/index.htm |date=20 August 2024 }}, from Franco Bampi's website, with links to the texts of the two decree laws</ref>

/><ref>''[http://www.polis.unige.it/rco/rapu/immagini/scelte/25-37%20gastaldi/25-69-aree%20centrali/aree%20centrali.pdf Il concorso per un piano regolatore di alcune zone del centro della città] Partially damaged by Allied bombing in World War II and only partially rebuilt in the immediate postwar period, the historic center was for several decades one of the most degraded areas of Genoa, immortalized as such by songs, books, and films. In the months following the end of the conflict, the very entrance to the area was discouraged to Allied soldiers present in the city, complete with warning signs in English placed at the entrances to the alleys in Sottoripa (some still visible, though partly erased), precisely because of the dangers that the underworld and widespread prostitution could pose to those who ventured, without knowing it, into the maze of alleys and rubble.<ref name="scrittealleati">[http://www.ilsecoloxix.it/p/genova/2008/12/29/ALXZDwJC-guerra_scritte_finiscono.shtml Le scritte della guerra finiscono sotto tutela] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161112084340/http://www.ilsecoloxix.it/p/genova/2008/12/29/ALXZDwJC-guerra_scritte_finiscono.shtml|date=12 November 2016}}, article from “Il Secolo XIX,” 29 December 2008</ref> The area of the Sarzano convent, one of the most heavily damaged by the bombings, became in the immediate postwar period a refuge for homeless people and immigrants,<ref>Riccardo Navone, ''Viaggio nei caruggi. Edicole votive, pietre e portali'', Fratelli Frilli Editori, Genova, 2007 ISBN 978-88-7563-334-9, p. 33</ref> a situation well depicted in the Oscar-winning film ''[[The Walls of Malapaga]]'' (1949). In the following decades, a number of building interventions led to the demolition of several parts of the historic center, while new buildings sprang up on the rubble of the bombed palaces, which stand out not only for their modern style but also for their greater height compared to the surrounding buildings.

[[File:Ruderi in Piazza delle Erbe Genova 01.jpg|thumb|left|Some ruins in Piazza delle Erbe, in the area where the oratory of Santa Maria del Suffragio once stood, among the few signs of World War 2 bombing to be present at the beginning of the 21st century (photo from December 2008). In 2010, a modern-style school building was built on the site, designed by architects [[Jörg Friedrich (architect)|Jörg Friedrich]] and Roberto Melai.<ref>[https://www.comune.genova.it/content/lrsquoopen-day-della-nuova-scuola-di-piazza-delle-erbe L'open day della nuova scuola di Piazza delle Erbe] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820131610/https://www2.comune.genova.it//content/lrsquoopen-day-della-nuova-scuola-di-piazza-delle-erbe |date=20 August 2024 }}, news from the official website of the municipality of Genoa, dated 8 March 2014</ref><ref>[https://genova.erasuperba.it/interviste/scuola-piazza-erbe-progettista-architetto-roberto-melai Scuola piazza Erbe, scelte tecniche e stilistiche: parola al progettista] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820131612/https://genova.erasuperba.it/scuola-piazza-erbe-progettista-architetto-roberto-melai |date=20 August 2024 }}, interview with designer Roberto Melai, from erasuperba.it, 26 November 2013</ref>]]

At the end of the 1960s, the area on Madre di Dio Street (where, in Passo Gattamora, there was [[Niccolò Paganini]]'s house) was demolished to allow the construction of the Centro dei Liguri executive complex. This is one of the last urbanistic changes (if not the last in absolute terms, certainly the last in importance) provided for in the 1932 master plan to actually be implemented.<ref name="viaggio50">Riccardo Navone, ''Viaggio nei caruggi. Gardens).<ref>[http://www.mentelocale.it/contenuti/index_html/id_contenuti_varint_19013 Giardini di plastica: riqualifichiamoli] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100109122851/http://www.mentelocale.it/contenuti/index_html/id_contenuti_varint_19013|data=9 gennaio 2010}}, Mentelocale.it article, dated 11 October 2007</ref> Also {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820131617/https://www.fondazioneansaldo.it/index.php/sopraelevata-una-strada-d-acciaio |date=20 August 2024 }} of the causeway, quoted from the After the construction of the nearby [[San Donato, Genoa|church of San Donato]] in the 12th century and [[Sant'Agostino, Genoa|church of Santa Tecla]] in the 13th century, part of this area of the city was again used for residential and commercial purposes, but it was not until the 16th century that intensive building of the area began.<ref>A cura di Piera Melli, ''La città ritrovata, Archeologia urbana a Genova 1984–1994'', Tormena Editore, 1996, p. 214 e sgg. ISBN 88-86017-62-6</ref> In the square, which owes its name to the open-air fruit and vegetable market there in the past, there is a marble fountain, with a [[putto]] at its top, made in 1697 by [[Domenico Parodi]].<ref>Federico Alizeri, ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=3kgZAAAAYAAJ&q=Guida+artistica+per+la+citt%C3%A0+di+Genova Guida artistica per la città di Genova]'', 1846, p. 315</ref>]]

The elevated road, a debated work whose possible demolition is speculated several times, running along the port arch of the city center, allows a view of part of the historic center from a panoramic position. Architect [[Renzo Piano]] suggested in 2007, in order to take advantage of this scenic route in the event of its demolition, to replace it with an overhead monorail.<ref>[https://ricerca.repubblica.it/repubblica/archivio/repubblica/2007/07/09/genova-sogna-la-metropolitana-aerea.html E Genova sogna la metropolitana aerea] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820131619/https://ricerca.repubblica.it/repubblica/archivio/repubblica/2007/07/09/genova-sogna-la-metropolitana-aerea.html |date=20 August 2024 }}, article from ''La Repubblica'' online, 9 July 2007</ref>

In 1976 a new master plan was approved by the municipality, which, among other things, aimed to attempt to rehabilitate the area.<ref>A.V., ''Interventi nel centro storico – Confronto fra esperienze operative'', edizioni Dedalo, gennaio 1978, ISBN 978-88-220-0339-3 [https://books.google.com/books?id=1zaeHQcWV1YC&dq=centro+storico+genova&pg=PA185 pp. 185–186] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820131624/https://books.google.it/books?id=1zaeHQcWV1YC&pg=PA179&dq=centro+storico+genova&hl=it#PPA185,M1 |date=20 August 2024 }}</ref> From the 1980s onward, partly due to funding related to events such as the [[1990 FIFA World Cup]], [[Genoa Expo '92]], the 2001 Genoa G8, and Genoa European Capital of Culture in 2004, a renaissance began, leading part of the old city to be one of the most popular tourist spots in Genoa. The [[Genoa Metro|subway itself]] has 5 of its 7 stations located in the old town area. During the various works carried out for the aforementioned events, traces of the old piers and ancient buildings have been found, but these, while bringing new information about the city's past, have almost always been covered over after being studied by the archaeologists of the superintendence and are therefore no longer visible.

In the different itineraries that unravel from [[Piazza De Ferrari]], the heart of the center, in an urbanistically unconventional nucleus, the result of multiple modifications and renovations over the centuries, it is possible to identify the three main guiding lines that trace, with the help of the fortresses and [[Walls of Genoa|walls]] built in different centuries between the Middle Ages, the Renaissance and the 19th century, the contours of an architecturally "oblique city" rich in unique and valuable elements.

These directions correspond, for the oldest part, to Via San Lorenzo, which descends, crossing numerous streets, alleys (the ''caruggi'') and lateral ''creuze'', from the Piano di Sant'Andrea and [[Piazza De Ferrari]] to the Marina and the old port. The pedestrianization of the square and the partial pedestrianization of the street, which took place in the early 21st century, make it the ideal pedestrian route for tourist flows between the port and the executive area. For the 16th–17th-century part in Via XXV Aprile, which, with the transit of Piazza delle Fontane Marose and [[Via Giuseppe Garibaldi (Genoa)|Via Garibaldi]] (the ancient Strada Nuova), leads to Piazza dell'Annunziata and the university district of [[Via Balbi (Genoa)|Via Balbi]] (home of the [[Palazzo Reale (Genoa)|Royal Palace]]). Finally, for the strictly medieval part, in the dense fabric of caruggi that from Piazza Campetto and the Macelli di Soziglia leads to the Church of [[Santa Maria delle Vigne]] and the Pre-Molo-Maddalena district.

After the revitalization of the area that occurred with the [[Genoa Expo '92]], the fulcrum around which many of the flows of commerce and tourism currently revolve is provided by the area of the old port (an area redesigned by [[Renzo Piano]]), where the [[Aquarium of Genoa|aquarium]] is located, with the back of Piazza Caricamento and the Sottoripa (or Ripa) arcades. From there, around the [[Bank of Saint George]] at which the city of merchants and dockers of the ''Compagnia dei caravana'' was being created, one can easily reach Via Orefici and Piazza Banchi, skirting the old [[Loggia della Mercanzia (Genova)|Loggia della Mercanzia]], site of the old Commodity Exchange, a building used for numerous events and exhibitions until 2021 and now home to an archaeological site.<ref>{{cite web |access-date=27 June 2023 |date=5 June 2023 |language=it |title=Cultura, alla Loggia di Banchi proseguono gli scavi archeologici |url=https://smart.comune.genova.it/comunicati-stampa-articoli/cultura-alla-loggia-di-banchi-proseguono-gli-scavi-archeologici |website=Comune di Genova {{!}} Sito Istituzionale |archive-date=27 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230627150456/https://smart.comune.genova.it/comunicati-stampa-articoli/cultura-alla-loggia-di-banchi-proseguono-gli-scavi-archeologici |url-status=live }}<!-- auto-translated from Italian by Module:CS1 translator --></ref>
