Confirming the recovery of the historic center in recent decades, or at least a substantial part of it, UNESCO declared part of the historic center a [[World Heritage Site]] on 13 July 2006.

== Landmarks and places of interest ==
The alleys that develop particularly in the part adjacent to the old port, constitute a kind of intricate [[Kasbah|casbah]] architecturally characterized in a way that is not always unified and easily identifiable, with [[Romanesque architecture|Romanesque-style]] churches, palaces of classical and neoclassical style and buildings belonging to the Middle Eastern culture, the result of the past that brought the Genoese to operate in the main ports of the [[Mediterranean Sea]] and on the fields of the [[Crusades]].

=== World Heritage Site ===
[[File:Flag of UNESCO.svg|45px|left|Patrimonio dell'Umanità dell'UNESCO]]
{{see also|Genoa: Le Strade Nuove and the system of the Palazzi dei Rolli}}

A large part of it, enclosed in the section of the so-called ''Strade Nuove'' ([[Via Giuseppe Garibaldi (Genoa)|Via Garibaldi]], Via Cairoli and [[Via Balbi (Genoa)|Via Balbi]]), where the [[Genoa: Le Strade Nuove and the system of the Palazzi dei Rolli|Rolli palaces]] stand, was declared a [[UNESCO World Heritage Site]] on 13 July 2006.

With the term ''Rolli'' (derived from the word ''scrolls''), or more precisely ''Rolli of the public lodgings of Genoa'', from 1576 onwards the lists of palaces that were excellent residences of the noble families who aspired to host, on the basis of a public draw, high personalities in transit for state visits, were indicated. Forty-two of these buildings were included in the World Heritage List.

The Rolli were divided into ''bussoli'', in which the buildings (about one hundred and fifty residences, not all of which still exist) were classified into three types of categories according to their prestige: the first was drawn up in 1576 and the next in 1588, 1599, 1614 and 1664.

On 20 January 2007, a plaque was placed by UNESCO at the beginning of Via Garibaldi with the motivation listing the series of Palazzi dei Rolli among the World Heritage Sites:

{{blockquote|The major mansions, varied in form and distribution, were drawn in official lists (''rolli'') to host state visits. The palaces, often erected on sloping ground, divided into a sequence of atrium – courtyard – staircase – garden and rich in interior decoration, express a singular social and economic identity that inaugurated modern-age urban architecture in Europe.}}

=== Religious architecture ===
[[File:Campanile sant Agostino Genova 01.jpg|thumb|The bell tower of the [[Sant'Agostino, Genoa|Church of St. Augustine]], photographed from Passo delle Murette. The cusp and four spires of the bell tower, similar in shape, and coeval in period of construction, to those of the Commenda of San Giovanni di Pré, are the only ones in Genoa to be covered with polychrome tiles, in the Moorish style of ''alicados''.<ref name="navone">Riccardo Navone, ''Viaggio nei caruggi. Edicole votive, pietre e portali'', Fratelli Frilli Editori, Genova, 2007 ISBN 978-88-7563-334-9, p. 31 e 32</ref>]]

Genoa's historic center is home to the largest and among the best-known churches and buildings of worship in the city. Of the very earliest churches that denoted the presence of Christian groups in the city virtually nothing remains, having been destroyed from time to time, incorporated into newer churches or heavily renovated over the centuries to the point of making the original scheme unrecognizable. The oldest churches visible today date from roughly the beginning of the late medieval period.

Symbols of Genoese religious power, but also of the noblest families who in most cases contributed to the establishment of many places of worship in the form of aristocratic chapels, the churches of the historic center are part of the history of Genoa and, from an architectural and touristic point of view, are a rallying point and attraction for the tourist-religious activity of the Ligurian capital.

As written earlier, with the establishment of the pro-Napoleonic [[Ligurian Republic]] following the [[Treaty of Campo Formio]] in 1797, many religious buildings were expropriated.<ref name= grandestoria6p141 /> After the annexation of the Republic to the [[Kingdom of Sardinia (1720–1861)|Kingdom of Sardinia]], decided during the [[Congress of Vienna]], some of these buildings remained state-owned while others were reassigned to the Catholic Church, but not always to the same religious orders that previously resided there. Major construction works, which took place in the city center from the early 19th century onward, then led to the demolition of several churches and monasteries, of which there are no visible traces left.

As for the formerly existing Islamic places of worship in the dock area, these were abandoned and used for other purposes at the end of the 18th century, when, in the wake of the ideals of the [[French Revolution]], the newly formed [[Ligurian Republic]] abolished slavery, freeing the Muslim prisoners there. Only a few remnants remain, incorporated into the building that houses the Faculty of Economics.<ref name=moschea1 /><ref name=moschea2 />

The Jewish community had several places of worship, both in the older city (as shown by the aforementioned letters of Theodoric from the early 6th century), and after the arrival of [[Sephardic Jews]] from Spain in the “ghetto” district, and later in the Pier district, which no longer exist. In 1935 the present synagogue was built, located in a side street of Via Assarotti (a steep slope that connects the [[Portoria]] neighborhood with the [[Castelletto (Genoa)|Castelletto]] neighborhood, in the area outside the historical center proper), which replaced the Molo one.<ref>[https://ricerca.repubblica.it/repubblica/archivio/repubblica/2001/09/01/il-placet-di-teodorico-restaurate-la-sinagoga.html Il placet di Teodorico Restaurate la Sinagoga] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231030112939/https://ricerca.repubblica.it/repubblica/archivio/repubblica/2001/09/01/il-placet-di-teodorico-restaurate-la-sinagoga.html |date=30 October 2023 }}, article in ''La Repubblica'', Genoa edition, 1 September 2001</ref>

=== The votive shrines and portals ===
[[File:Tabernacolo di San Giovanni Battista Genova Soziglia 02.jpg|thumb|[[John the Baptist|St. John the Baptist]] in Soziglia Square, [[Aedicula|aedicule]] dating from the 17th/18th centuries and restored in 1991.]]
{{blockquote|There are plenty of Saints' and Virgin's Shrines, of course; generally at the corners of streets.|[[Charles Dickens]] speaking of Genoa, "''Pictures from Italy''", 1846<ref name=pianoregolatoresociale>{{cite web |access-date=22 April 2021 |archive-date=19 December 2012 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20121219065356/http://www.pianoregolatoresociale.comune.genova.it/portal/page/categoryItem?contentId=467735 |title=Edicole votive e portali – Cosa sono? |url=http://www.pianoregolatoresociale.comune.genova.it/portal/page/categoryItem?contentId=467735 |website=Piano Regolatore Sociale della città di Genova}}<!-- auto-translated from Italian by Module:CS1 translator --> from the website of the Social Master Plan of the City of Genoa.</ref>}}

One of the typical features of Genoa's historic center is the large number of [[Aedicula|votive shrines]] present, not all of which are in a good state of preservation or easily visible, although a challenging restoration and cataloguing project has been underway in recent decades. The tradition originated in the late Middle Ages and continued for several centuries until the early 20th century, peaking in the 16th and 17th centuries.

Hundreds of aedicules (not all of which exist today) are believed to have been built in the historic center over time, many of them dedicated to Our Lady (particularly venerated in Genoa, so much so that in 1637 she was declared the “Queen of Genoa”), whether by [[Albergo (family)|nobles]], merchants and artisans, confraternities or ordinary citizens. The depictions present were then often adorned with [[Ex-voto|votive offerings]] and candles.<ref name="pianoregolatoresociale" /><ref name="comuneedicole">[https://web.archive.org/web/20060608173000/http://www.comune.genova.it/portal/template/viewTemplate?templateId=0w7j0py3k3_layout_6rl47oy3k5.psml Percorso turistico delle edicole votive], from the old Genoa City Council website.</ref><ref>[https://webthesis.biblio.polito.it/541/ Edicole votive fra centro antico e museo] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820131709/https://webthesis.biblio.polito.it/541/ |date=20 August 2024 }}, Carige Foundation article on votive shrine display at St. Augustine Museum</ref><ref>[http://www.frillieditori.com/books/viaggiocaruggi_intro.htm Presentazione del libro Viaggio nei Caruggi – Edicole votive, pietre e portali] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080509122333/http://www.frillieditori.com/books/viaggiocaruggi_intro.htm|data=9 maggio 2008}}, by Riccardo Navone, Fratelli Frilli Editori</ref>

Another feature are the portals of palaces, finely decorated with sculptures, statues (in marble, slate and stone) and frescoes. The origin of the spread of this type of portals is to be found in the 15th century, when the noble families who owned the palaces in the area, in order to cope with the shortage of space for new living areas or to be used as stores, decided to reuse the courtyards and porticos of the same, changing the distribution of space and obtaining new rooms and [[loggia]]s overlapping them.

The redefined palaces thus needed new entrances, more sumptuous than the previous ones, the design and construction of which were entrusted to sculptors and master masons, often from outside the city (many of whom came to Genoa because they were interested in the marble and other raw materials that were landed in the port), mainly from [[Lombardy]] (from the Intelvi Valley) or [[Tuscany]]. The themes depicted, besides religious ones, often took up Greek mythology or were tributes to the family that owned the palace.<ref name="pianoregolatoresociale" /><ref name="comuneedicole" />

In the decades-long deterioration that accompanied the downtown area, many of the statues contained in the aedicules and many of the decorations on the portals deteriorated severely or were subject to theft and vandalism.

== Genoa's growth and population trends in the old city ==
Genoa's population at the beginning of the 16th century is estimated at between 50,000 and 100,000, depending on different estimates (the most recent ones being less), included almost entirely in the ''sestieri'' of Molo, Maddalena, Prè and Portoria.<ref name="annuario">Statistical Yearbook 2006, a publication of the ''Statistical Organizational Unit of the City of Genoa.''</ref>

An 1834 text, ''Viaggio nella Liguria marittima'' (Journey in Maritime Liguria), written by Davide Bertolotti, gives a table in which he summarizes data dating from about 1530, collected by “il Giustiniano” ([[Agostino Giustiniani]], bishop of Nebbio, author of the ''Castigatissimi Annali di Genova''), and based on these he tries to obtain an estimate of the population in the first decades of the 16th century. According to Giustiniani's data reported and summed up by Bertolotti, there were 6298 houses in Genoa in the circle included within the sixteenth-century walls, to which must be added more than 300 houses in the area that would be incorporated into the seventeenth-century ''Mura Nuove''. The humblest houses, believed to be the majority, would have had 4, 5 or 6 ''fuochi'' (i.e., family units, normally of 5 or 6 people): this leads the nineteenth-century writer to estimate (considering a default estimate of four ''fuochi'' per house and 5 individuals per ''fuoco'') the population of Genoa (wall circle plus surroundings) to be about 132,000, a figure higher than the values generally considered correct for that period by present-day historians.<ref>Davide Bertolotti, ''Viaggio nella Liguria marittima'', 1834, [https://books.google.com/books?id=vSGy_dNcWMgC&pg=RA2-PA217 pag 217] e [https://books.google.com/books?id=vSGy_dNcWMgC p. 218] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820133321/https://books.google.it/books?output=html&id=vSGy_dNcWMgC&jtp=218&hl=it |date=20 August 2024 }}</ref><ref>Agostino Giustiniani (version with notes by Giovanni Battista Spotorno), ''Annali della repubblica di Genova'', 1854, [https://books.google.com/books?id=X70O38FhZdwC p. 59 e sgg.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820133328/https://books.google.it/books?lr=&output=html&id=X70O38FhZdwC&jtp=59&hl=it |date=20 August 2024 }}</ref>

Estimates and studies based on various documents (annals, documents of the Bishopric and the Republic of Genoa, etc.) reported by the publications of the Municipality's Statistical Organizational Unit, suggest a population of nearly 50,000 in the second half of the 16th century, which would grow until of the plague of 1656, reaching about 90,000 residents, only to collapse because of it to about 40,000. The expansion of the city in the meantime would also incorporate into it the sestieri of San Vincenzo (to the east) and San Teodoro (to the west).<ref name="annuario" />

From the mid-sixteenth century onward, after the plague, the population would increase again, reaching about 100,000 in the 1830s, to exceed 130,000 one forty years later.<ref name="annuario" /> The aforementioned ''Dizionario geografico storico statistico commerciale degli Stati di S.M. il Re di Sardegna'' by Goffredo Casalis, reporting data for 1938, estimated the city's population, military (both garrison soldiers and naval personnel) and port personnel included, at 115,257. The author also specifies that there were 181 Jews who “not being able to own any real estate, engaged in maritime trade with good success,” and had a synagogue in the area of the Malapaga walls (Molo ''sestiere''); in addition to these, the author reports, there were also several Protestants, 296 Swiss and 65 Anglicans, and these groups "were mostly engaged in commerce, and figured among the bankers, and the richest shopkeepers" and had a church in the area of the Crosa del Diavolo (present-day Largo San Giuseppe, in the vicinity of Galleria Mazzini and Piazza Corvetto). Casalis also specifies that Genoa usually had an average number of outsiders estimated at about 2,800, to which were added the inhabitants of nearby areas who came to the city during daylight hours for business or work.<ref>Goffredo Casalis, [https://books.google.com/books?id=eXEPAAAAYAAJ Dizionario geografico storico statistico commerciale degli Stati di S.M. il Re di Sardegna Volume 7] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820123029/https://books.google.it/books?id=eXEPAAAAYAAJ&hl=it |date=20 August 2024 }}, [https://books.google.com/books?id=eXEPAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA824 pag 824] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240820133215/https://books.google.it/books?id=eXEPAAAAYAAJ&hl=it&pg=PA824#v=onepage&q&f=false |date=20 August 2024 }}</ref>

As far as the period between the 18th and 19th centuries is concerned, in 1797, by [[Napoleon|Napoleon Bonaparte]], the [[Republic of Genoa]] ended its existence and with it the de facto independence of the city. The subsequent [[Ligurian Republic]] was closely dependent on the French, alongside whom it fought several wars that led to its besieging by the Austrians and British in 1800, a siege that caused nearly 10,000 deaths due to malnutrition and disease.<ref>[http://www.francobampi.it/liguria/blocco/miscosi.htm Il Blocco di Genova] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231030112842/http://www.francobampi.it/liguria/blocco/miscosi.htm |date=30 October 2023 }}, by Giulio Micossi, reported on Franco Bampi's website.</ref> The Ligurian Republic itself would be annexed to the [[First French Empire|French Empire]] in 1805, and with the fall of the French Empire in 1814, after a few months as the Genoese Republic, it would then be annexed to the [[Kingdom of Sardinia (1720–1861)|Savoy Kingdom of Sardinia]].

The population census of 1861 reported the existence of 5409 houses, 185 of which were empty, a number of households amounting to 28931, with a population within the course of the walls of 139,993 (de facto population, i.e., present on the census date 31 December 1861, of 127,986 inhabitants, to which must be added 12,007 absentees), of whom, however, only 127,735 actually resided (de jure population) in Genoa.<ref name="ottocentogenovese">''Ottocento Genovese'', [https://web.archive.org/web/20140707054218/http://statistica.comune.genova.it/pubblicazioni/statistiche.php Pubblicazioni dell'Unità Organizzativa Statistica del Comune di Genova], p. 15</ref> In the census a decade later, in 1871, the de facto population rises to 130,269, while the de jure population falls to 125,606. The bureau analyzing the data from the 1871 census justified this decline by changes in the unstable population, by the cholera epidemic that had hit the city between 1866 and 1867, and by the fact that many citizens had moved to the more livable and inexpensive neighboring towns.<ref>''Ottocento Genovese'', [https://web.archive.org/web/20140707054218/http://statistica.comune.genova.it/pubblicazioni/statistiche.php Pubblicazioni dell'Unità Organizzativa Statistica del Comune di Genova], p. 123 e sgg.</ref>

In 1874 Genoa grew out of its initial 6 ''sestieri'' and annexed, in its expansion to the east and along the Bisagno valley, precisely these municipalities: Marassi, [[Albaro|San Francesco]] and San Martino d'Albaro, San Fruttuoso, and Staglieno, as well as that of the Foce (a name referring to the presence of the estuary of the [[Bisagno (river)|Bisagno]] stream).<ref name="annuario" />

As also pointed out in the Demographic Atlas published by the municipality,<ref name="atlante2007" /> the ancient area of the historic center, corresponding to the Prè-Molo-Maddalena sestieri, shows a singular demographic evolution with respect to the rest of Genoa: albeit with some fluctuations between one census and the next one, the population appears to have slightly decreased between the first one in 1861 and the one almost a century later in 1951, to then have its own and true collapse between the 1961 and 1971 census (−12. 060 residents), during the period when instead the city as a whole reached its population peak (816,872 residents at the 1971 census), and then continued to decline (this time consistently with the rest of the city) in the censuses of the following decades. At the 2001 census, the population in the Prè-Molo-Maddalena area, with its 19,453 residents, corresponds to about 3.19 percent of the total city population (610,307 residents), while considering all the ''sestieri'' it comes to about 18.08 percent. However, for several decades there has been a substantial presence of irregular immigrants in the area, which, in fact, makes the actual population higher than recorded by statistics.

extract:
The historic center of Genoa is the core of the old town organized in the maze of alleys (caruggi) of medieval origin that runs – from east to west – from the hill of Carignano (Genoa) to the Genova Piazza Principe railway station, close to what was once the Palazzo del Principe, residence of Admiral Andrea Doria. Urbanistically, the area is part of Municipio I Centro-Est.
However, the current municipal area was created by the merger, which took place on several occasions starting in the second half of the 19th century, of historic Genoa with adjacent municipalities and towns (now neighborhoods), some of which have more or less ancient historic centers of their own and have been urbanistically transformed over the years.
The major urban planning operations carried out from the first half of the 19th century to beyond the middle of the 20th century (which are difficult to replicate today, given the increased interest in the protection of historic neighborhoods by the public administration), combined with the damage that occurred during World War II (many of the old buildings were destroyed during the Allied bombing raids), partly disrupted the original fabric of the historic center. Slightly less than a quarter of the buildings (23.5 percent) date from the postwar period or later.
